title: Jabil Develops New Resilient Supply Chain Portfolio
content:
Jabil Develops New Resilient Supply Chain Portfolio
Prioritise Us
on Google
Jabil is offering supply chain management and procurement consulting with its new portfolio. Credit: Getty
Jabil has developed a unified Procurement & Supply Chain Services portfolio, expanding global sourcing capabilities and supplier access
Jabil has consolidated five acquired businesses into a single Procurement & Supply Chain Services portfolio. The move brings together ProcureAbility, Retronix, ID8 Global, Velocity Electronics and Rebound Electronics under one operational structure.
The company operates more than 120 sites across the globe and employs 3,500 procurement and supply chain professionals. Jabil maintains relationships with more than 40,000
suppliers through its network
, providing customers with access to a broad range of sourcing options and procurement capabilities.
The engineering and manufacturing solutions provider acquired ProcureAbility and Retronix in 2023. ID8 Global was launched as a joint venture with Cyferd Inc in 2024. Velocity Electronics and Rebound Electronics were both acquired in 2025.
Responding to market volatility
The consolidated offering addresses challenges including component shortages, geopolitical uncertainty and tariff pressures. Jabil will deliver services ranging from procurement consulting and component sourcing to supply chain management and global distribution.
Frank McKay
is Senior Vice President and Chief Supply Chain Officer at Jabil. Speaking at Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit 2026, Frank said: "All the disruptions that have happened with the geopolitical environment, semiconductor shortages and everything that occurred throughout COVID meant that our customers expected us to have built-in optionality, processes and policies in place."
The portfolio aims to provide visibility across procurement operations and sourcing channels. Companies using the service will access Jabil's supplier network as an extension of their internal procurement teams, enabling them to respond more quickly to supply chain disruptions and market changes.
Frank McKay, Chief Supply Chain Officer at Jabil explores the Procurement & Supply Chain Services portfolio
At a glance
60 years of Jabil experience across industries
More than 120 sites worldwide
3,500 procurement and supply chain professionals
More than 40,000 global suppliers in the Jabil network
Jabil leverages a US$25bn annual procurement spend
Expanding procurement and distribution capability
ProcureAbility adds procurement consulting and managed services to Jabil's operations. The business continues to operate independently following its acquisition and offers expertise in procurement optimisation.
Retronix brings more than 30 years of experience in component recovery services. The company provides reballing, retinning and authenticity testing that could extend component lifecycles and reduce waste in electronics manufacturing.
ID8 Global combines data technology with AI to operate an autonomous procurement and supply chain platform. The joint venture helps organisations manage logistics, sourcing and operations at scale.
Velocity Electronics has almost three decades of experience as an independent distributor. The business supplies sourcing and inventory management solutions to original equipment manufacturers and contract manufacturers.
Rebound Electronics adds independent distribution and aftermarket fulfilment to Jabil's portfolio. The acquisition could help customers secure components in constrained supply markets and maintain production continuity during periods of shortage.
Strengthening component sourcing networks
The combined businesses operate within Jabil's existing supply chain infrastructure. Jabil has 60 years of experience across multiple industries and provides engineering, manufacturing and supply chain solutions to brands worldwide.
Frank says: "We're giving our customers more options, better visibility and stronger support as they work to secure critical supply and build long-term operational resilience.
“These acquisitions strengthen the way we support customers in a market that's only getting more complex. They expand our global electronic component capabilities and supply chain services, but more importantly, they give more businesses access to Jabil's supply chain and procurement expertise, supplier network and operational discipline."
The company states it is committed to building processes that reduce environmental impact. Jabil operates in
communities worldwide and provides solutions
it describes as scalable and tailored to individual customers.

We're giving our customers more options, better visibility and stronger support as they work to secure critical supply and build long-term operational resilience.

title: DP World Expands Shipping Network for Operational Resilience
content:
DP World Expands Shipping Network for Operational Resilience
Prioritise Us
on Google
DP World is launching a new trade route | Hong Yong Chang Sheng Docked at Jebel Ali. Credit: DP World
DP World is strengthening supply chain resilience through the launch of its China Africa Link, explains Ganesh Raj, Global COO, Marine Services at DP World
DP World is undergoing a period of expansion, with the launch of the China Africa link.
Around the world, shipping is becoming more complex and more unreliable. As a result, businesses are
forming new trade routes
in order to simplify shipping and add new options for their clients.
The launch of this new route is strengthening maritime connections and offering access to new and expanding markets.
Logistics growth
DP World's Shipping Solutions AMEA business (Shipping Solutions) is launching the China Africa Link, a weekly service which aims to increase connectivity between the Far East and Africa. This allows customers to gain more of a choice with shipping, alongside wider market access and greater resilience in their supply chains.
In recent years, changing trade relationships and the growing pressure from climate change have resulted in unstable supply chains. By limiting shipping routes, businesses are more at-risk of disruption – trade routes can be unpassable, new legislation can make entry points costly.
"Global trade is changing, and our customers need more than shipping capacity. They need reliable connections, greater choice and the flexibility to adapt as trade patterns evolve,” explains Ganesh Raj, Global COO, Marine Services at DP World.
Ganesh Raj, Global Chief Operating Officer, Marine Services at DP World. Credit: DP World
Through expanded options, businesses can choose the optimal route for them, which can save money, time and help them navigate turbulence more effectively. The China Africa Link is scheduled to begin in late November 2026, which will strengthen connectivity between China and the growing markets in East and Southern Africa.
At a glance
DP World moves 10% of global trade every day
It has a TEU global capacity of 110 million
85 countries around the world are served by DP World
More than US$10bn has been invested in DP World’s global logistics network
DP World is undertaking a US$165m expansion of its Maputo container terminal
Trade connectivity
The service will include a strong port rotation, with a route of: Shanghai (China) – Ningbo (China) – Nansha (China) – Port Klang Westport (Malaysia) – Dar es Salaam (Tanzania) – Maputo (Mozambique) – Singapore – Shanghai (China).
Through this, there will be more connections between key African markets and critical Chinese export gateways. As a result of this route, there will be greater movement of goods across established and emerging trade routes. This creates greater variety and shows an investment into new routes, helping grow logistics capabilities and
supporting economies in a new way
“The new China Africa Link demonstrates how we are bringing our Connected Trade Corridors approach to life,” Ganesh adds.
“By strengthening maritime connectivity between China and Africa, we are opening up more opportunities for businesses and creating smarter, more flexible shipping networks that help keep cargo moving."
The link is a part of DP World Marine Services' Connected Trade Corridors approach, a widespread aim of bringing together maritime solutions, ports and inland transport. In doing this, DP World is creating more flexible trade networks that are more integrated and more resilient.
Through increased connectivity into African gateways, DP World is making use of a growing market. Alongside that, customers will gain additional routing options, which results in growing trade flows and strengthened links between regional and international markets.
This supports a resilient global trade flow, demonstrating how businesses can operate an extensive network. Economic growth in Sub-Saharan Africa is increasing, so trade links to the region are critical. The continent is growing into a strong hub for commerce, so DP World’s development of the trade link comes at a critical time for the region.
DP World's China Africa Link. Credit: DP World
Global trade is changing, and our customers need more than shipping capacity.
Ganesh Raj, Global COO, Marine Services at DP World
Expanding capabilities
African trade is growing, driven by increased access to international markets and increased exports of metals and agricultural products. In the past year, the adoption of AI and digital infrastructure has taken place across the continent, allowing for the wider growth of business opportunities.
The China Africa Link will support the ongoing movement of a range of goods, including electronics, construction materials, automotive components and machinery. There will also be the movement of African exports, including minerals, agricultural products and other materials.
DP World is making ongoing investments into African trade infrastructure, demonstrating its awareness as a growing trade hub. This includes a US$165m expansion of its Maputo container terminal in Mozambique, which aims to double its current handling capacity.
In Tanzania, the company is modernising the Port of Dar es Salaam with a US$500m investment. These show that DP World is working to connect marine services and port infrastructure across the continent in order to
strengthen regional connectivity
and do its part to grow capabilities in South-South trade.

DP World
DP World is a leading global supply chain and logistics company headquartered in Dubai, UAE. Operating in over 60 countries across six continents, it manages ports, terminals, and logistics operations worldwide. The company facilitates international trade by handling cargo, container shipping, and freight services. DP World plays a crucial role in connecting businesses to global markets through innovative infrastructure solutions and smart logistics technology, making it essential to modern commerce.

LogiPharma is the premier pharmaceutical supply chain conference bringing together industry leaders, logistics professionals, and healthcare innovators. The event focuses on addressing critical challenges in pharmaceutical distribution, cold chain management, and regulatory compliance. Attendees explore emerging technologies, serialization, temperature-controlled logistics, and strategies for improving efficiency while maintaining product integrity. Founded by Bruce McLaren in 1963, the company has won multiple F1 championships and produces cutting-edge high-performance vehicles through McLaren Automotive. Combining aerospace-grade materials with advanced engineering, McLaren creates iconic models like the 720S and P1. The brand represents innovation, speed, and precision engineering at motorsport's highest level.

Arab Health is the largest healthcare exhibition and medical conference in the Middle East, held annually in Dubai. It attracts over 55,000 healthcare professionals, manufacturers, and distributors from 160+ countries. The event showcases cutting-edge medical technology, equipment, pharmaceuticals, and healthcare solutions. Arab Health serves as a crucial platform for regional and international business development, featuring specialized conferences on medical innovation, digital health, and emerging healthcare trends across the MENA region.
Porsche Motorsport
Porsche Motorsport represents the racing division of Porsche AG, with legendary success spanning decades in endurance racing, Formula E, and GT competitions. Known for dominating Le Mans with 19 overall victories, Porsche engineers high-performance race cars that influence production vehicle development. The department manages factory racing programs, customer racing support, and develops iconic models like the 911 GT3. Porsche Motorsport embodies racing heritage, technical excellence, and winning tradition.

title: Exiger Secures US Air Force ICBM Supply Chain Risk Contract
content:
Exiger Secures US Air Force ICBM Supply Chain Risk Contract
Prioritise Us
on Google
A Minotaur I rocket carrying an unarmed Mk21A reentry vehicle launches from Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, 17 June 2024. The Mk21A program is overseen by the Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center. (U.S. Space Force photo by Senior Airman Kadielle Shaw)
VP of Nuclear Security Scott LaFoy outlines how Exiger's services will increase component and supplier visibility in extended defence supply chains
Exiger, a market-leading supply chain risk management company, has been awarded a US$12 million contract by the US Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center. The contract focuses on enhancing the Intercontinental Ballistic Missile (ICBM) Systems Directorate by delivering advanced multi-tier supply chain illumination and deep Defence Industrial Base (DIB) analytics.
"Ensuring 24/7 readiness in lockstep alongside strategic modernization is one of the most consequential missions in U.S. national security. This requires both the long-term orchestration of multiple strategic, sensitive supplier bases while very actively mapping and mitigating adversarial threats to the supply chain," says Scott LaFoy, Vice President of Nuclear and Technology Security Programs at Exiger.
"Exiger’s differentiated strength is our ability to connect supplier risk to the parts, materials, facilities, and industrial base dependencies that actually drive mission readiness and program performance."
Scott LaFoy, Vice President of Nuclear and Technology Security Programs, Exiger
EO 14415 and the DoW
The upcoming entry into force of Executive Order 14415 - effective mid-January 2027 - requires the US Department of War (DoW) to map the critical supply chains behind goods and services acquisitions. While the exact of scope of mapping requirements has yet to be announced by the DoW, EO 14415 directs the DoW to develop a policy requiring prime defence contractors as well as lower tier contractors at any tier to map critical supply chains for selected acquisitions.
A prime contractor may therefore need evidence from a tier 1 supplier. That supplier may in turn need information including purchases of goods, materials, systems, software and services from sub-tier suppliers who have no direct DoW contract.. As such, EO14415 extends the potential scope of mapping requirements beyond defence contractors to dual-use component suppliers, for example. Exiger has relevant experience with mapping product, part and material dependencies across the defence supply chain.
Exiger’s approach will help the ICBM Systems Directorate identify obsolescence risk, single-source dependencies, supply chain fragility, vendor viability concerns, counterfeit or Diminishing Manufacturing Sources and Material Shortages-affected components, workforce gaps, and supplier readiness issues. The platform will also provide predictive analytics to support part obsolescence forecasting, vendor behaviour tracking, forecasted inventory action timelines, and risk mitigation planning.
Key facts about indentured Bill of Materials
Mapping multi-tier defence supply chains to ensure absolute compliance with Executive Order 14415.
Inventorying and normalising existing Bill of Materials, software Bill of Materials (SBOM), part, drawing, supplier and material data.
Connecting critical parts and materials to the suppliers and sub-tiers beneath them.
Identifying foreign-source, material, capacity, sole-source and concentration exposures.
Connecting raw materials with raw-material origin, with additional supplier and lifecycle information attached to those elements.
EO 14415 directs the Department of War to develop deeper supply chain mapping, supplier vetting, mitigation, and source-qualification requirements for selected national security acquisitions.
Key Partners
Exiger is a globally recognised technology provider specialising in supply chain risk management and advanced multi-tier analytics. Their proprietary software illuminates deeply hidden vulnerabilities across complex vendor networks.
US Department of War
The US Department of War heavily utilises massive technological investments to digitally transform military logistics. By enforcing rigorous mandates like Executive Order 14415, the DoW is helping to increase the resilience and robustness of defence supply chain networks.
US Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center
The US Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center is responsible for the lifecycle management of the US's nuclear arsenal.

title: Baringa: Planning AI Sovereignty in Critical Supply Chains

Baringa: Planning AI Sovereignty in Critical Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
EXA’s Chicago-to-Istanbul route shows the scale of global AI connectivity. Credit: Getty Images
Baringa is collaborating with Cosine to develop AI for highly regulated areas and to strengthen UK resilience, explains Edward Sharkey, Partner at Baringa
In an era of major AI adoption, even critical supply chains are making use of the technology in order to drive efficiency.
Critical infrastructure, government and financial services are all integrating the tools into their operations, working to maintain resilience amid ongoing volatility.
AI in these sectors
needs to be developed with experts in these sectors, which is why Baringa and Cosine are partnering to ensure strict governance and operational outcomes at the same time.
Developing resilience
Global consulting firm Baringa works to blend industry expertise and advanced technology in order to help its clients deliver exceptional results. It works across energy, financial services, government, retail, pharmaceuticals and life sciences, telecoms and more.
It works directly with its clients to ensure it makes a positive impact on the world, having worked across sustainable operations and
supply chain resilience
. Baringa operates under the policy that AI and cloud technology are not absolute when it comes to driving value, but that they need to be tailored to each business’ needs.
It makes use of its AI solutions, cloud technology and industry experts in order to unlock new insights and accelerate innovation across global supply chains. Through collaborative efforts, such as its latest with Cosine, Baringa is contributing to the development of AI for critical infrastructure in the UK. For these organisations, AI is a question of national capability. This partnership, and others, aims to drive innovation across the nation in order to strengthen its standing and increase efficiency in operations.
“We are delighted to announce our partnership with Cosine,” Edward Sharkey, Partner and Global Head of AI & Solutions at Baringa, explains.
Edward Sharkey, Partner and Global Head of AI & Solutions, Baringa
”Generative AI offers our clients a step change in productivity, but for many, the real question is not what the technology is capable of, it is the boundaries within which their most sensitive data must remain. Together with Cosine, we help clients unlock the value of Generative AI without compromising on control, security or sovereignty of their critical data.”
At a glance
The UK Government has a £500m Sovereign AI programme
The open letter calls for a commitment of more than £20bn over the next five years to secure sovereign AI use
Baringa uses AI to enhance and accelerate business-wide operations
The aim of the partnership is to develop resilience across the sector
Baringa has 25 years of experience in management consulting
AI sovereignty and reliability
Alongside this partnership, Cosine published an Open Letter to the UK Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, supported by a coalition of executives across defence, financial services and critical national infrastructure. The letter argued that Britain should take on a more strategic approach to AI, stating that it guides reliability, strategy, resilience and influence.
The open letter states, “countries that lack those capabilities risk becoming dependent on decisions, infrastructure and operating conditions determined elsewhere.”
In April, the UK Government announced its £500m (US$670m) Sovereign AI programme. This programme is a national effort to support British founders and drive growth across British AI development, alongside supporting the creation of jobs in that field. A large part of the programme is to keep expertise, decision making and economic value within British operations, rather than relying on foreign tech giants.
Supply chain collaboration
The wider partnership between Cosine and Baringa is to develop AI across critical infrastructure. Baringa will help test and enhance Cosine’s model, aiming to shape how Lumen Sovereign – the UK’s first sovereign frontier AI model – can operate amid strict governance, enhanced security and niche legacy systems.
Alistair Pullen, CEO of Cosine says: “Critical infrastructure needs AI capability that reflects the realistic conditions in which the work happens. That means complex systems, long-lived assets, high-consequence decisions, strict governance and no room for unexplained dependencies.
Alistair Pullen, CEO of Cosine
“Baringa brings deep energy-sector knowledge and practical experience turning AI and digital systems into operational outcomes. Its contribution will help us shape Lumen Sovereign around the requirements of the organisations that keep the UK energy system running.”
Supply chain leaders are assessing the role of AI in their operations, but much of it is sourced from other countries. Baringa is working with Cosine to develop a reliable
AI model which is regulated
, making it more secure. The partnership explores the role of sovereign AI in the supply chain, with a focus on sectors which need to be reliable at all times – such as the energy sector and government services.
Critical infrastructure needs AI capability that reflects the realistic conditions in which the work happens.
Alistair Pullen, CEO of Cosine
Key Partners
Baringa is a leading independent management consultancy founded in 2000, headquartered in London. The firm specializes in energy, financial services, retail, telecoms, and government sectors. Known for combining deep industry expertise with analytics and technology capabilities, Baringa helps organizations navigate complex transformations, improve operations, and drive sustainable growth. With over 1,000 employees across multiple international offices, they deliver strategic advisory and implementation services to major corporations and public sector clients worldwide.
Cosine is an AI-powered software development company that creates coding assistance tools using machine learning. Their flagship product, Genie, acts as an AI software engineer capable of understanding codebases, fixing bugs, and implementing features. Founded to enhance developer productivity, Cosine leverages large language models to automate routine coding tasks. The company represents the emerging intersection of artificial intelligence and software engineering, aiming to augment human developers rather than replace them, improving code quality and development speed.
BT Group (British Telecommunications) is the UK's largest telecommunications and network provider, founded in 1846. Operating brands including EE, Plusnet, and BT Business, the company serves millions of consumers and businesses with mobile, broadband, TV, and phone services. BT manages critical national infrastructure, including extensive fiber-optic and 5G networks. Listed on the London Stock Exchange, BT is undergoing digital transformation, investing heavily in full-fiber broadband rollout and modernizing legacy systems while maintaining its position as a telecommunications industry leader.
Xcelo Group is a business services provider specializing in finance, procurement, and technology solutions for mid-market and enterprise clients. The company offers outsourced accounting, financial management, procurement services, and digital transformation support. With expertise across various industries, Xcelo helps organizations streamline operations, reduce costs, and improve financial performance. They combine process optimization with technology implementation, providing scalable solutions that adapt to client needs, enabling businesses to focus on core activities while Xcelo manages essential back-office functions efficiently.

unveiled the Yangwang Altior, its new ultra-luxury EV with coach doors, over 1,000 km of CTLC range, a 1,000V fast-charging platform, and plenty of premium extras.

The Atrio is Yangwang’s largest and most luxurious sedan, set to compete with high-end brands like Rolls-Royce, Bentley, and Mercedes-Benz Maybach.
Measuring 5,600 mm long, 2,030 mm wide, and 1,590 mm tall, with a 3,500 mm wheelbase, BYD’s flagship sedan sits squarely between the Rolls-Royce Ghost and Phantom (standard wheelbase) in length.
BYD said the “Golden Body Proportions” are designed to maximize interior space for both front and rear passengers.
Its meticulous front-end design is inspired by “Ding,” a traditional ancient Chinese cauldron, featuring “diamond-cut” headlights, a 137-gemstone dot-matrix grille, and, to top it off, a 24K pure gold car emblem sits up front and center.
BYD Yangwang Altior ultra-luxury sedan (Source: BYD)
The coach doors create a grand entrance, with the front doors opening at an 80-degree angle and the rear doors opening to a 90-degree angle.
Inside, the flagship sedan takes luxury up a notch with a massive, full-length panoramic center infotainment screen that extends from the driver to the passenger side.
BYD Yangwang Altior interior (Source: BYD)
The “Wrap-around cockpit” is designed to create an immersive, premium experience, with four executive seats and a central island for rear passengers that includes vehicle controls, storage, and even a champagne glass holder.
BYD said it offers the most second-row space in its class, but didn’t reveal specifics. The zero-gravity “cloud-like” rear seats feature a four-ball mechanical massage head, you know, for those longer trips.
Meanwhile, the front passenger seat can fold at the push of a button to open up more space for rear passengers.
The interior features premium materials, including full-grain genuine leather seats, diamond-cut detailing, real wood trim, and natural lambswool foot pads.
And that’s not all. It also has a 39-speaker Dynaudio Platinum Evidence high-end sound system that creates an immersive 360-degree “hall-level” sound experience.
The Yangwang Altio is packed with BYD’s latest breakthrough tech, including a high-speed tire-blowout stability system, emergency float mode, and in-place U-turn or tank-turn control using its quad-motor e4 platform.
It also uses BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Fast Charging Technology, which provides a CLTC driving range of over 1,000 km (621 miles).
The flagship sedan features “extremely fast flash charging,” BYD said, thanks to its 1000V ultra flash charging tech. It takes just five minutes to charge the vehicle’s battery from 10% to 70%. To go from 10% to 97% it takes just nine minutes.
BYD opened orders for the limited-edition “Mountain and River Rhyme” Yangwang Altrio model, which will be extremely exclusive with just 399 units.
Buyers can place a reservation with a 300,000 yuan ($45,000) deposit. BYD didn’t reveal final prices, but the global version is expected to start at around 2 million yuan ($300,000).

title: LiveWire just showed off its biggest electric motorcycle lineup yet
content:
Electric Motorcycles
LiveWire
Micah Toll
| Nov 9 2026 - 7:13 am PT
Customized version of the LiveWire S4 Honcho displayed at EICMA 2026
LiveWire
has spent the last few years expanding beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off. But seeing the company’s latest machines all together at EICMA in Milan really drives home just how much broader LiveWire’s ambitions have become.
I stopped by the LiveWire booth at EICMA 2026, where the company had everything from its new lightweight S4 Honcho models to the freshly acquired DUST electric dirt bikes – plus STACYC’s electric balance bikes for the youngest riders.
It’s quite a spread, and perhaps more importantly, it paints a picture of a company that increasingly wants to have an electric two-wheeler for just about every stage of a rider’s life.
I also had a chance to spend several hours test-riding the S4 Honcho Street in Milan, so be on the lookout for that article and video to experience it with me.
But for now, let’s see what was at the LiveWire booth.
LiveWire S4 Honcho takes center stage
Perhaps the most important bikes at the booth were the S4 Honcho models, LiveWire’s new lightweight and lower-cost electric motorcycles.
The production S4 Honcho Street
made its European debut
at EICMA alongside the dirt-oriented S4 Honcho Trail. The Trail version recently began reaching customers in the US, with the Street now en route to dealerships, and European sales are beginning around the EICMA launch.
These bikes represent a significant departure from LiveWire’s earlier strategy. Instead of trying to compete directly with full-size gasoline motorcycles on outright performance, the Honcho platform is aimed at riders looking for something smaller, simpler, and more approachable.
And now the family is getting even bigger.
Also on display was the new S4 Honcho Skate, making its first public appearance.
The Skate is planned for 2027 and further expands the modular Honcho platform with a stripped-down, playful design.
For those who have followed H-D’s electric ambitions for as long as I have, you might even remember the original
Harley-Davidson electric moped prototype
that seems to have served as inspiration for the Honcho Skate’s design.
Seeing the various Honcho versions together also makes LiveWire’s strategy with the platform much clearer. Rather than creating one small electric motorcycle, the company is building an entire family around the concept.
DUST Moto officially becomes part of the family
The other major attraction at LiveWire’s booth was the DUST lineup.
LiveWire acquired the assets of DUST Moto earlier this year,
bringing the lightweight electric dirt bike company under its umbrella. EICMA marked the first public showing of the production-intent DUST Hightail under LiveWire ownership.
The Hightail had already generated plenty of interest before the acquisition as a lightweight, high-performance electric dirt bike. Now we’re getting our first look at how that machine fits into LiveWire’s broader plans.
The company is targeting a 2027 introduction for the production Hightail.
But it wasn’t alone.
LiveWire also showed the new DUST Spur, another model planned for 2027 and intended to expand the newly formed DUST family.
The DUST acquisition is particularly interesting because it gives LiveWire an immediate foothold in the rapidly growing lightweight electric off-road motorcycle space without having to develop an entirely new platform from scratch.
Fast charging coming to the S2 line?
In what could be a hint at faster charging to come, there was an interesting S2 Alpanista Corsa motorcycle that had been outfitted with a NACS plug and DC fast-charging capabilities.
LiveWire claimed a 20-80% charge in under 10 minutes, which would revolutionize the ability to do long-distance motorcycle touring, or just make it more convenient to get a quick charge and head back to your apartment.
There’s on word on whether the concept will make it to production, but the specs are enticing!
The most interesting part of LiveWire’s EICMA display may not have been any individual motorcycle, but rather what happens when you stand back and look at the entire booth.
On one end you’ve got STACYC electric balance bikes. LiveWire says the brand has already introduced more than 250,000 riders to two wheels.
Then you’ve got the lightweight S4 Honcho family. Above that sit the DUST machines for more serious off-road riding, while LiveWire’s existing S2 motorcycles continue to cover the higher-performance street end of the spectrum.
That’s becoming something of an electric two-wheeler ladder.
A kid can theoretically start on a STACYC, graduate into increasingly capable electric two-wheelers, and eventually wind up on a proper electric motorcycle – all within the same corporate family.
And that feels particularly relevant at a show like EICMA, where much of the motorcycle industry is still trying to figure out exactly where electric motorcycles fit.
LiveWire seems increasingly convinced that the answer isn’t simply to build electric replacements for existing gasoline motorcycles.
Instead, the company is spreading out into categories where electric drivetrains can create different kinds of motorcycles altogether.
Electrek’s Take
I’ve been following LiveWire’s evolution for years, and the company standing in front of me at EICMA looks considerably different from the one that started out selling
a single expensive flagship electric motorcycle.
The big, high-performance bikes are still important, but machines like the S4 Honcho and DUST Hightail are arguably more interesting to me because they can bring entirely different riders into electric motorcycling.
They’re smaller. They’re simpler. And perhaps most importantly, they’re targeting the kind of fun, accessible riding that doesn’t require superbike levels of performance.
There’s still plenty we need to learn about several of these new models, particularly final specifications and pricing for the 2027 machines.
But seeing the Honcho, Honcho Skate, Hightail, Spur, and STACYC machines together at EICMA makes one thing pretty clear: LiveWire isn’t just trying to sell a few electric motorcycles anymore.
It’s trying to build an entire electric two-wheeler ecosystem.

title: Tesla launches Robotaxi in San Antonio with a 274 sq mi geofence on paper
content:
Robotaxi
Tesla Robotaxi
Fred Lambert
| Nov 9 2026 - 6:36 am PT
Tesla is launching its Robotaxi service in San Antonio, its eighth city, with a launch geofence covering about 274 square miles. That’s the biggest day-one map Tesla has ever posted, and more than four times the size of Waymo’s San Antonio service area.
But if Tesla’s recent maps are any guide, a big chunk of that area won’t be bookable. In Austin, an independent check found the Robotaxi app only accepted pickups and drop-offs in about 59% of the zone Tesla advertises.
A big map, and no cars spotted yet
Tesla’s official Robotaxi account made the announcement just after midnight local time: “Robotaxi available in San Antonio starting tomorrow, 5am.” It came with a map of the “launch geofence,” a large polygon that runs from Loop 1604 on the north side down to just south of downtown.
Robotaxi Tracker
, which measures operator maps and logs fleet sightings, puts the zone at 274 square miles. That covers about 1.0 million residents (51% of the metro) and 721,000 jobs. San Antonio International Airport sits inside the polygon, but it isn’t served.
Waymo started driverless rides in San Antonio in February with more than 60 square miles and opened to all riders in October, airport trips included. Robotaxi Tracker currently lists Waymo’s San Antonio area at 59 square miles.
What Tesla didn’t say is how many cars will cover its 274 square miles. As of Monday morning, Robotaxi Tracker hadn’t logged a single Tesla Robotaxi in San Antonio.
The launch landed the same day Tesla expanded Austin again. The tracker now measures Tesla’s Austin zone at 443 square miles, up 178 square miles since mid-September.
The map isn’t the service
We’ve seen this movie. Last month, Tesla
expanded its Houston geofence into the shape of a rocket
, and within two days the creator of Robotaxi Tracker
found the app refusing downtown pickups inside it
Since then, Koby Pierce, who tracks Tesla’s service on X, has done the tedious work of checking city after city. He searched thousands of real addresses in the Robotaxi app on an emulator and mapped only the ones where Tesla allows a pickup or drop-off, then compared that with the map Tesla advertises. Here’s the share of Tesla’s advertised land area that actually works:
Austin: about 59% (83% of residents)
Miami: 61% (67% of residents)
Orlando: about 70%
Fort Worth: about 72%
Houston: about 74%
Dallas: 78% (89% of residents)
Austin's dropoff/pickup Geofence is ~41% smaller than advertised.
Seems mostly the East side of town is inaccessible. Unsure the cause. Any ideas?
Dallas is next and should be done by noon tomrrow.
Austin is the one that matters. It’s Tesla’s flagship market, with 453 unsupervised vehicles in service according to Robotaxi Tracker. Yet about 41% of the advertised map Pierce tested, mostly on the east side of town, wouldn’t take a ride request. Pierce points to railroad crossings as a big factor in several cities, which lines up with the strange downtown routing we saw in Houston.
To be fair, Pierce says Waymo is next on his list, and he expects “they’re no better.” Robotaxi Tracker already had to trim Waymo’s Orlando area last month after finding the airport, inside Waymo’s published map, wasn’t selectable. We’ll look at those numbers when they’re out. But it doesn’t change what Tesla is doing with San Antonio today.
Electrek’s Take
Credit where it’s due. A 274-square-mile launch in a new city is progress, and Tesla now runs unsupervised rides in eight cities. At the start of this year, it had no unsupervised rides anywhere.
But we need to stop taking Tesla’s geofence numbers at face value, and that includes us. We used Tesla’s 254-square-mile figure for Houston, and it turned out to be overstated. In all six cities Pierce has checked, the real service area is between 59% and 78% of what Tesla posts. In Austin and Miami, it’s about 60%.
So the honest way to read the San Antonio announcement is “up to 274 square miles.” In practice, expect something closer to 160 to 210 square miles, with an unknown number of cars, and the airport already off the table. That’s still bigger than Waymo’s 59 square miles in the city.
The problem is that square miles are the metric Tesla fully controls. Drawing a polygon costs nothing, and the numbers were all over X within hours of the post. Cars per square mile, wait times, and rides completed are much harder to inflate, and nationally Waymo still runs over 4,000 driverless vehicles to Tesla’s 666, per Robotaxi Tracker.
I still consider this a small pilot by any standard, and safety remains the bottleneck. Tesla is still forcing riders through hour-long rides that should take 15 minutes because they have to take routes that avoid areas that Tesla can’t safely navigate without supervision.
Until that’s fixed, robotaxi won’t be able to meaningfully scale beyond these limited demonstrations in geo-fenced areas.

title: Musk says Cybertruck isn't dying from weak sales — the numbers disagree
content:
Tesla Cybertruck
Fred Lambert
| Nov 9 2026 - 5:56 am PT
Tesla Cybertruck production April 2024
Elon Musk now claims Cybertruck orders “far exceed” Tesla’s production rate, and that the truck isn’t being killed because it’s unprofitable. It’s his second explanation in three days for ending the pickup.
The problem is that Tesla’s own numbers say the opposite. The Cybertruck line has been running at roughly a quarter of its installed capacity, and Tesla spent all of 2026 discounting, re-trimming, and repricing the truck to find buyers.
Here’s what Musk posted on X overnight:
“The Cybertruck order rate far exceeds our production rate. We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people. This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media, but rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.”
The Cybertruck order rate far exceeds our production rate. We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.
This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported…
https://t.co/rGmNKV3ILs
He was quote-tweeting a Tesla fan telling people to “get it while you can.” So yes, this is also a sales pitch.
On Friday, Musk
announced Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production
at Giga Texas around mid-2027 “to make room for increased Cybercab production.” That was the first story. Now it’s about “complexity” and “opportunity cost.” Let’s go through it.
“Order rate far exceeds our production rate”
Tesla controls its production rate. That’s the flaw in this claim.
Tesla built the Cybertruck supply chain for 250,000 units a year, and its latest shareholder letter still lists more than 125,000 units of installed capacity. In Q3 2026, it delivered 8,295 “Other Models.” With Model S and Model X out of production,
we estimated 7,000 to 8,000 of those were Cybertrucks
. That’s a 30,000-a-year pace, down 48% year-over-year in that category.
If orders had been outrunning production at any point this year, Tesla had about 95,000 units of idle annual capacity sitting right there. It didn’t use it.
And companies with a backlog don’t behave like Tesla did. In February, it offered a dual-motor Cybertruck at $59,990 for “only the next 10 days.” It pulled a single-motor RWD version after just 173 sales. It leaned on Musk’s own companies too:
SpaceX bought 1,279 Cybertrucks in Q4 2025
, about 19% of US registrations that quarter once you add his other firms.
Cox Automotive estimates US Cybertruck sales fell from 14,416 in Q3 2024 to 3,519 in Q1 2026 and 3,744 in Q2. It’s a demand problem everyone could see.
So if orders spiked this weekend, there’s an obvious reason: Musk told the world on Friday that the truck is going away. A last-call rush on a discontinued vehicle is not proof that it was selling.
“Will have to return deposits for a lot of people”
Tesla has been sitting on Cybertruck deposits it was never going to fill for years.
Musk touted more than a million reservations, and crowdsourced tallies
put the list near 2 million by 2023
. Its best US quarter, by Cox Automotive’s estimate, was 14,416 trucks. The reservation book was a vanity number, not an order book.
Two weeks ago, Tesla
cancelled the Cybertruck for Australia and New Zealand
and refunded deposits people had paid in 2019. Returning deposits is something Tesla was already doing because it couldn’t sell the truck in those markets, not because it was swamped.
“Not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable”
This one is a straw man. Our reporting, and most of the coverage Friday, was about sales, not margins. The truck sells at about 12% of the volume Tesla planned for.
Tesla doesn’t disclose Cybertruck margins, so Musk can say whatever he wants here and nobody can check it. But he’s the one who said in 2023 that Tesla had “dug our own grave with Cybertruck” because of how hard it was to build profitably.
And look at what Tesla did the same day it announced the end of production: it
raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10%
and paused orders for the cheapest trim. The cheapest orderable Cybertruck went from $69,990 in early August to $92,490. You do that to squeeze margin out of the last trucks, not because the line was printing money.
The “opportunity cost” argument proves our point
Follow Musk’s logic to the end. If the Cybertruck were profitable and orders really outran production, killing it would mean walking away from guaranteed profit for a robotaxi that had 463 units registered in Texas as of late October and no proven business yet.
The only way that trade makes sense is if the Cybertruck’s profit at 30,000 units a year is small. Which is another way of saying it doesn’t sell enough.
Giga Texas also has more than 10 million square feet of floor space, and the Cybercab runs on its own “unboxed” line. Tesla can’t make use of the Cybertruck line and floor space was never the constraint. To further adapt his logic for shutting down Cybertruck production, Musk shifted his argument from “space” to Cybercab’s line needing some “smart people”, who he implied work on the Cybertruck.
Musk wrote on Saturday that
“there are a very limited number of smart, dedicated people”
, but Michael So, who led Cybercab new product introduction and was Giga Texas employee #1, left in April for nuclear startup Aalo Atomics. Last month,
Tesla lost its Cybercab general assembly lead to Rivian’s R2 program
just weeks after the launch. If talent is the bottleneck, it’s the Cybercab team that’s bleeding it.
Electrek’s Take
Musk doesn’t want the Cybertruck to go down in history as a flop, and we get it. It’s his truck. He approved the controversial design, hyped it for four years before it shipped, and boasted that 1 million reservations could translate to 500,000 units a year.
But you can’t run a line at a quarter of capacity, run “10 days only” discounts, pull trims after 173 sales, and sell trucks to your own rocket company, then turn around and tell people demand was never the issue. The data is public. Tesla’s own delivery reports are public.
Our read on what happened is simple. Demand collapsed in 2025 and never came back. Tesla tried every pricing trick it had. When nothing worked, it found a future-facing reason to end it, and now it’s spinning the inevitable end-of-life rush as proof the truck was a hit all along.
Musk loves a big TAM. SpaceX’s IPO filing put its total addressable market at
$28.5 trillion
, and last month he went further, writing that he sees
“a path to SpaceX being worth orders of magnitude more than the current Earth economy.”
So apply the same lens to Tesla. Pickups are one of the biggest and most profitable vehicle markets on the planet. Ford sold 801,525 F-Series trucks in the US last year, GM sold 925,656 Silverados and Sierras combined, and Ram moved 374,059. That’s more than 2.1 million trucks from three automakers, easily north of $100 billion a year at today’s transaction prices.
Robotaxis? Waymo, by far the leader, is doing about 500,000 paid rides a week, and analysts estimated its revenue run rate at roughly $355 million earlier this year. Tesla doesn’t even break out robotaxi revenue and we expect it to be a fraction of Waymo’s.
Maybe that flips one day. But that’s the bet here: Tesla is walking away from a giant market it can sell into today for one that only gets big if autonomy is solved in the next couple of years. Musk has made that exact bet before. He promised a million robotaxis on the road by 2020 and has said unsupervised self-driving was a year away almost every year since 2016. He’s lost every time.
And that rush is real, for what it’s worth. Some people want the last of a weird, genuinely impressive truck. That doesn’t make it a business.

title: Electric dirt bikes keep getting called e-bikes. The bicycle industry wants that to stop
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Nov 9 2026 - 4:54 am PT
The line between electric bicycles and electric motorcycles has been getting increasingly blurry – though perhaps not because the vehicles themselves are actually that hard to tell apart.
Instead, much of the confusion comes down to terminology. High-powered electric dirt bikes capable of reaching motorcycle-like speeds are increasingly being referred to as “e-bikes,” despite sharing relatively little with the low-speed electric bicycles millions of Americans use for commuting and recreation.
Now the U.S. bicycle industry is asking federal regulators to make that distinction much clearer.
PeopleForBikes
, the bicycle industry’s leading trade association, recently testified before the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC), calling for stronger federal regulations that specifically distinguish electric bicycles from higher-powered e-motos and electric dirt bikes.
“E-bikes and e-motos are fundamentally different products, and federal safety regulations need to reflect that distinction,” explained PeopleForBikes Policy and General Counsel Matt Moore. “When high-powered electric dirt bikes are marketed as e-bikes, it creates confusion for consumers and puts the credibility of legitimate e-bikes at risk.”
The Lectric XP4 is typical of a street-legal electric bicycle, unlike e-motos that greatly exceed electric bicycle limits
There’s a real nomenclature problem hiding underneath all of this. The term “e-bike” is widely used as shorthand for “electric bicycle,” but it isn’t exclusively used that way. Motorcycles have been called “bikes” for generations, and motorcycle media and riders will sometimes casually refer to electric motorcycles as “e-bikes” too, just in the way a biker refers to his Harley as his “bike”. In fact, it all comes from the same root. We don’t call motorcyclists “motorists”, do we? No… we call them “bikers”.
All of that makes phrases like “legal e-bike” and “legitimate e-bike” that were even used by PeopleForBikes in its arguments somewhat problematic when discussing proposed regulation. The term “e-bike” simply doesn’t mean anything specific, at least not legally.
What actually matters from a legal standpoint is whether a vehicle meets the codified definition of an electric bicycle, not whether someone calls it an e-bike – especially when the term e-bike is practically applied so broadly. In other words, perhaps part of separating electric bicycles from e-motos is being more precise with the terminology ourselves: “electric bicycle” has a specific regulatory meaning, while “e-bike” has increasingly become a much fuzzier colloquial term. As much as some would want the term “e-bike” to mean something with pedals, it simply doesn’t – at least not in North America.
I’m certainly guilty of this myself in my writing and videos, falling back on the commonly used phrasing instead of the technical legal terminology, but keeping them separated could help with the growing misunderstanding in the industry.
Legal electric bicycles are a far cry from e-motos, but the terminology can often get mixed up
That distinction has become increasingly important as lightweight electric motorcycles and dirt bikes
have exploded in popularity
. Many feature bicycle-like frames and components, and some
even include pedals
, but their performance can extend far beyond what federal law defines as a low-speed electric bicycle.
The concern goes beyond mere semantics. When a 50-60 mph (80-100 km/h) electric dirt bike gets lumped into the same category as a 20-28 mph (32-45 km/h) commuter e-bike, crashes and reckless riding involving the former can quickly become part of the public conversation surrounding the latter. That can ultimately influence how lawmakers, regulators, police departments, and the general public view e-bikes as a whole.
In fact, many of the supposed electric bicycle crash figures we’ve seen touted in the news aren’t from electric bicycles at all, but rather from e-moto accidents that have been lumped in with electric bicycles, making the latter appear more dangerous than they truly are.
If street-legal electric bicycles were separated from e-motos in crash statistics, the category would be revealed to be much safer than conventional reporting would have us believe.
E-motos like this Annioki A9 can sometimes look similar to electric bicycles, despite hiding much higher performance
All of this and more has led to PeopleForBikes pushing federal regulators to draw a clearer line.
As part of its CPSC testimony, the organization recommended retaining the existing federal definition of a low-speed electric bicycle while creating a separate definition for e-motos, including machines capable of speeds up to 60 mph (96 km/h). It also called for mandatory electrical safety standards for off-road e-motos, which it says currently fall into a regulatory gap, as well as greater scrutiny of conversion kits capable of turning conventional bicycles into vehicles operating beyond their original structural design limits.
The testimony came as the CPSC considers
new mandatory federal battery safety standards for e-bikes and other electric mobility devices
. PeopleForBikes says it supports stronger battery standards, while recommending that regulators rely on existing UL standards without modification.
PeopleForBikes is also asking the CPSC and National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to coordinate enforcement against e-motos that evade federal requirements.
None of this means e-motos are inherently bad. They’re incredibly fun machines, and there’s a rapidly growing market for them. But a 60 mph (96 km/h) electric dirt bike isn’t an electric bicycle simply because it looks vaguely like one.
And increasingly, the bicycle industry wants regulators to make sure everyone understands the difference.
E-motos like the Juiced Nomadix can be great fun, but are meant to be used off of public streets. Keep it in the dirt!

title: A degree in Paris, a gigawatt at the border - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
How French winter temperature reshapes cross-border flows, day-ahead prices and solar revenue in the markets around it.
09 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
High-voltage pylon at the Col de Vernant in commune of Arâches-la-Frasse, Haute-Savoie, France.
When France gets cold, its neighbours feel it at the border. Each degree of French winter cold takes about 1 GW off French net exports and goes with day-ahead prices €5 ($5.6)/MWh to €7/MWh higher in France, Belgium and Germany. Roughly half of the French price response, a third of the Belgian and a quarter of the German is French temperature on its own rather than the neighbours’ weather. Eleven winters of data can also say why the loss sits in the hours solar cannot fill, why the nuclear fleet rather than the thermometer decides whether France keeps exporting, and why a cold spell can leave a solar plant better off.
01. One cold spell, and the pattern of eleven winters
The winter of 2025/26 showed the whole mechanism in four weeks. Between 15 and 21 December 2025, with the French effective temperature, a population-weighted average of the day’s temperature and the two days before it, at 9.8 C, France exported a net 16.3 GW on average to its six neighbours. Between 29 December and 11 January, at 1.9 C, it exported 5.7 GW. On 6 January, at −1.5 C and with French demand averaging 82 GW over the day, France imported a net 3.7 GW. Nuclear output was 52.4 GW in the mild week and 53.3 GW in the cold spell, wind averaged 7.2 and 7.5 GW, and French solar averaged no more than 2.3 GW on its best day of the cold spell. The swing in exports was therefore driven by demand, which rose from 56 GW to 72 GW between the two windows. Lower exports covered about 10.6 GW of that 16 GW rise. The remaining 5 GW or so was met mostly by gas, with smaller gains in nuclear, hydro, solar and wind.
8 GW to 9 GW between a mild day and a cold one
That cold spell is close to the average pattern of eleven winters, counting November to March as winter. On the mildest tenth of winter days, above 11.6 C, France exports 9.0 GW. On the coldest tenth, below 3.2 C, it exports close to zero. Measured within each winter rather than across all eleven, the swing is 8.3 GW, so the loss between a mild day and a cold one is 8 to 9 GW whichever way it is measured. Germany loses 2.1 GW of French supply between the two, on physical flows that include loop flows, Belgium 1.9 GW, Switzerland 1.7 GW, Britain 1.3 GW, Spain 1.1 GW and Italy 1.0 GW, and on the German, Belgian and Spanish borders the flow reverses on average. On cold days the Belgian, German and Swiss borders run near their highest winter import levels in 5 to 6% of hours, against under 1% on mild days. In a cold spell the question shifts from how much France can export to how much it can take in.
02. Where the degree goes
Both the December spell and the eleven-winter average put the swing down to demand, so the share of the extra demand that is met at home decides how much of the loss crosses the border. French demand starts to respond to cold below 15.5 C. Within a winter, once month, weekday and holidays are allowed for, it rises by 1.8 GW for every degree colder. That response has not weakened, at 1.7 GW per degree in 2015/16 and 1.9 GW in 2025/26. Between 15.5 C and freezing, demand climbs by about 30 GW. Below 2 C the average winter day turns France from exporter to importer.
Of the 1.8 GW a degree adds within a winter, nuclear output is 0.43 GW higher, gas 0.36 GW, hydro 0.20 GW, coal and oil 0.11 GW, and net exports 1.04 GW lower. Wind falls by 0.35 GW, as cold French days tend to be still ones, so that loss has to be covered as well, and the five supply terms add up to the 1.8 GW rise in demand plus the 0.35 GW lost from wind. Solar shows no response to temperature within a winter. At 1.04 GW per degree, a winter 1 C colder than the 7.8 C average would remove about 3.8 TWh from net exports.
The neighbours are cold on the same days
The obvious objection is that the neighbours are cold on the same days, so the flows reflect their weather as much as France’s. Holding their temperatures and the French and German wind and solar forecasts fixed gives a larger export response, not a smaller one. The reason is that the neighbours’ own cold pulls French power across the border on the same days, which partly hides the loss in the raw figures. With those controls in place, French demand rises 1.48 GW per degree of French cold rather than 1.8 GW, nuclear output no longer moves with the French thermometer, and 1.29 GW of that 1.48 GW is met by lower exports. The 0.43 GW of nuclear uplift per degree in the raw figures therefore goes with the neighbours’ pull on French supply rather than with French cold itself. The 1.04 GW is the figure for a winter in which the neighbours are cold at the same time, as they usually are; the 1.29 GW is the French temperature effect alone, and it falls almost entirely on the borders. The split between French and neighbouring cold is approximate, because the two move together.
Each border loses between 0.16 and 0.28 GW per degree
On that basis, Belgium loses 0.28 GW per degree of French cold, Germany 0.26 GW, Switzerland 0.21 GW, Italy and Britain 0.19 GW and Spain 0.16 GW, and the six borders sum to the 1.29 GW. Belgian and French effective temperatures move almost in step, so Belgium’s coldest days and the loss of French supply arrive together.
03. The fleet decides how much France can spare
The per-degree figures describe an average winter. Whether France keeps exporting through a particular cold spell depends on what the nuclear fleet is producing when the cold arrives, and the coldest fortnight of each winter shows what France could still spare. In December 2022, at 2.2 C with nuclear output at 40 GW, France imported 8.0 GW. In January 2025, at 3.0 C with nuclear output at 55 GW, it exported 7.2 GW. The coldest fortnight of 2025/26, straddling the turn of the year, was colder than both, at 1.3 C, and France exported 5.9 GW with 54 GW of nuclear output. Cold of much the same depth has produced a 15 GW range in French net exports. Even with nuclear output at 55 GW, the deepest cold of the eleven winters, 0.7 C in January 2017, pulled France into import, though only by 2.0 GW.
The seasonal balance tells the same story. It was −4 TWh in 2021/22 and close to zero in 2022/23, the two winters with nuclear output averaging 42 GW or less. It reached 44 TWh in 2025/26, a winter that was milder than average and had 49 GW of average nuclear output. France was a net importer on 58% of winter days in 2021/22 and on 1% in 2025/26.
04. Solar in a French cold spell
French solar output has more than quadrupled since 2015, so the natural question is whether it can fill any of that winter gap. Its share of French winter generation has risen from under 1% to 3.2%, but December and January output has been 26% to 37% of the summer before it in every year since 2015.
On the coldest tenth of winter days French solar averaged 1.0 GW against 1.3 GW on the mildest, and German solar, on the day-ahead forecast, 2.0 GW against 3.7 GW. The coldest days cluster in December and January, when days are shortest. Within those two months a cold day has more French solar than a mild one, so the lower output on cold days is a matter of the calendar, not of the cold. In the last two winters French solar covered 2.6% of demand on the coldest days. Doubling capacity would take that to about 5%, against a 23 GW gap in demand between the mildest and coldest tenth of winter days.
The loss sits in the hours solar cannot reach
Estimated hour by hour, the export loss peaks at 1.18 GW per degree at 08:00 and at 1.10 GW at 19:00. Both are hours in which winter solar output is close to zero. French demand itself responds least to cold in mid-afternoon, and the export loss follows it, with a trough of 0.93 GW at 15:00.
05. Price formation on a cold French day
On the coldest tenth of winter days the French day-ahead price averaged €113/MWh, against €61/MWh on the mildest. The neighbours moved with it. Belgium averaged €111/MWh against €66/MWh and Germany €101/MWh against €66/MWh, and the French premium over Germany flipped from −€5/MWh on mild days to 12 €/MWh on cold days. Gaps measured across all eleven winters depend on which winters the cold days happen to fall in, and without 2022/23 the French gap is €38/MWh rather than €52/MWh, so the per-degree response, estimated within each month of each winter, is the better guide.
Per degree of French cold, estimated within each month of each winter, the French baseload price rises €6.7/MWh, the Belgian €6.0/MWh, the German €5.3/MWh, the Dutch and Swiss €4.7/MWh, the northern Italian €3.2/MWh and the Spanish €2.8/MWh. In every winter since 2015 the French price rise per degree has been between 4% and 9% of that winter’s average price.
Holding the neighbours’ temperatures and the wind and solar forecasts fixed, as in the export estimate, the French response falls to €3.7/MWh, the Belgian to €2.0/MWh and the German to €1.4/MWh. On these estimates, roughly half of the French price response, a third of the Belgian and a quarter of the German is French cold on its own, and the rest comes with the neighbours’ own cold and the low wind that arrive on the same days.
Within the day, the French price response peaks at €8.0/MWh per degree at 08:00 and €8.4/MWh at 18:00. The Belgian and German curves follow the same shape. The night hours respond least, and midday responds less than either peak.
Capture rates rise on cold days; revenue depends on geography and on what has been sold
That shape has a consequence for solar. The capture rate is the average price solar receives divided by the average price for all hours. It rises in all seven zones on the coldest tenth of winter days compared with the mildest, and reaches parity or above everywhere except Spain. France moves from €0.92 to €1.03, Belgium from €0.93 to €1.03, Germany from €0.96 to €1.05, the Netherlands from €0.91 to €1.04, Switzerland and northern Italy from €0.98 to €1.03, and Spain from €0.82 to €0.97. With little solar on a cold day there is no midday surplus to push the price down, and the first solar hours fall just after the morning peak, when prices are still high, so the price solar receives rises faster than the average and ends up above it. The French solar capture price doubles, from €58 to €118, and the Dutch almost doubles, from €73 to €142.
The price data cover fewer winters than the flow data, and on their cold days solar output is 28% lower than on their mild days in France, 42% lower in Belgium and 52% lower in Germany, a slightly larger drop than in the eleven-winter comparison. Taking average capture price multiplied by average output, French solar earned 47% more per day on the coldest days than on the mildest, because the price gain outran the output loss. Spanish solar earned 13% more and Belgian solar 8% more. German solar earned 15% less, even with baseload prices more than 50% higher, because the output loss was larger than the price gain. Whether a portfolio gains or loses depends as much on how much winter output it has already sold, and in what hourly profile, as on where the plant sits. A producer who has sold a fixed winter volume forward is short that output on exactly the days when buying it back costs most, and the buyer of a pay-as-produced contract holds the opposite position. On these data a cold spell is not a capture-rate problem for winter solar but a volume one.
The storage spread moves from the solar cycle to the overnight cycle
A battery that charges on cheap midday solar and discharges into the evening trades the midday-to-evening spread. That spread narrows on cold days, from €27/MWh to €20/MWh in France and from €34/MWh to €17/MWh in Germany, because the midday price rises with everything else once there is no solar to push it down. The overnight-to-morning spread moves the other way, from €30/MWh to 43 €/MWh in France and from €28/MWh to €41/MWh in Germany between mild and cold days, because the night hours respond least and the morning peak responds far more. A cold spell therefore moves the day-ahead spread a battery can trade in winter from the solar cycle to the overnight cycle rather than removing it, and a battery able to cycle twice a day can trade both.
06. Conclusion
Eleven winters of data make French winter cold a measurable quantity for the markets around it. Each degree takes about a gigawatt off French exports, the six neighbours share that loss, and the French price response has stayed between 4% and 9% of the winter price level in every winter since 2015, including the crisis winters. A model of Belgian or German winter prices that carries local temperature but not French temperature leaves out roughly a quarter to a third of the price response to a French cold day.
For solar, winter output is set by the calendar rather than by the cold, and cold-day prices rise, so the exposure sits in how winter output has been sold rather than in the capture rate. For storage, a cold spell moves the earning window from the midday-to-evening cycle to the overnight-to-morning cycle.
Two forces pull in opposite directions over the coming winters. A fuller French fleet leaves more to export through a cold fortnight, as the last two winters show. Against that, the French demand response per degree is no lower than it was eleven winters ago, at 1.9 GW in 2025/26 against 1.7 GW in 2015/16. Solar growth does little for the peaks in which the loss and the price response are largest. The balance between fleet availability and demand decides whether the next cold spell looks like the turn of 2025/26, with France still exporting 5.9 GW through its coldest fortnight, or like December 2022, with France importing 8.0 GW.
How WSP’s Electricity Market Outlook can help
WSP’s Electricity Market Outlook (EMO) is designed to analyse these market dynamics. The underlying PRIMES model has supported European Commission energy-policy analysis for more than two decades and simulates all major European electricity markets simultaneously through to 2050. Cross-border flows are derived using a replication of the EUPHEMIA algorithm used in Europe’s single day-ahead coupling. Model outputs include hourly wholesale prices, capture rates, negative-price frequency and depth, curtailment exposure, interconnector utilisation and BESS profitability projections at both country and asset level. These outputs provide the quantitative basis for winter risk assessment, PPA and CfD bid analysis and long-term storage revenue modelling.

title: Key takeaways from RE-Source 2026 in Amsterdam - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Europe’s corporate renewable energy buyers and sellers have shifted their focus from price to risk allocation as negative prices erode solar-only contracts and battery-backed hybrid deals move to the center of the market, according to discussions last week at RE-Source 2026 in Amsterdam.
Brian Publicover
09 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
The Beurs van Berlage, a former commodities exchange on the avenue between Amsterdam’s central train station and main square, was built more than a century ago so the city’s merchants had somewhere to agree on prices. But the 1,400 or so people who filled the cavernous red-brick hall on Nov. 4 and 5 came to negotiate deals for renewable electricity, a commodity whose price falls below zero for a growing number of hours each year.
The 10th edition of RE-Source, organized by SolarPower Europe and WindEurope through their joint RE-Source Platform, brought more than 350 corporate energy buyers to some 400 prescheduled meetings with suppliers. But the deal flow they were chasing is thinning: the RE-Source Platform said corporate power purchase agreements (PPAs) have secured 5.9 GW of renewable capacity in Europe so far in 2026, down 9.7% on the same period last year.
Francesco Rossetto, a policy officer at the EU Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators (ACER), presented the agency’s annual PPA assessment and described “a market that is cooling down a little bit.” He said activity peaked in 2024 and has held near 2025 levels since. Meanwhile, the share of hours with very low power prices has climbed from 1% to 2% in 2021 to about 10%.
Solar is taking the brunt. Max Plumptre, director of European transactions at Seattle-based PPA marketplace LevelTen Energy, said capture rates – the share of the average market price a solar plant actually earns – have roughly halved in Spain and Germany since 2022.
Swiss market intelligence firm Pexapark said
standalone solar PPA volumes have fallen 43%
this year, and that Italy has overtaken Spain as their largest market, largely because Spanish activity has collapsed. Almost one-quarter of Spanish solar output has been generated during negative-price hours, according to the research firm.
Itamar Orlandi, director of commercial strategy at Pexapark, said solar prices “started to go into free fall about three years ago and that free fall still hasn’t stopped.”
Buyers are responding by asking for more than one technology. Plumptre said nearly every request for proposals on LevelTen’s platform this year has included a hybrid product “in some sort of fashion,” and about 25% of offers in its
latest quarterly report
were hybrid.
Pexapark said PPAs combining several technologies have almost doubled, while Rossetto said capture rates for solar paired with storage are diverging from those for solar alone.
Hybrid hedging
For insulation maker Rockwool, the shift is practical. Kenneth Dupont, energy category director for the Danish company, said it moved away from single-technology PPAs because they do not fit factories that run around the clock. He advised buyers to contract about half of their demand through PPAs and cover the rest with renewable energy certificates.
Spain shows why storage is now central. Silvia Escudero, head of upstream and downstream origination Iberia at
Statkraft
, noted that the country has logged about
920 hours of zero or negative prices
so far this year. With grid connections scarce, she said, putting batteries behind existing solar connections is by far the fastest route to market. However, she warned buyers that a battery’s flexibility carries an opportunity cost, because grid services can be worth more than delivering power to a customer. “A hybrid PPA is not a solar PPA with a battery, it’s much more complex than that,” said Escudero.
That complexity is where traders see their opening. Kristina Herold Høgh, director of RETO origination and contract management at Centrica Energy, said
new contract structures for batteries
are emerging. Profile swaps, which convert a renewable plant’s variable output into a delivery shape that suits the buyer, are becoming more standard.
Herold Høgh cast traders as “problem solvers” that bring the risk capital and credit these deals require. One gap remains in recognizing stored power: one panelist said only one or two European countries issue guarantees of origin, the certificates that prove renewable sourcing, for stored electricity.
Domenico Franceschino, head of origination for West and East Europe at Axpo Solutions, explained how a battery’s location shapes its value, using indicative figures for
tolling agreements
in France, under which an offtaker pays a fixed fee for control of the battery. For seven- to 10-year contracts starting in 2029, he put annual fees at about €80,000 ($89,500)/MW for a standalone battery, €65,000/MW for a co-located unit that can also charge from the grid and €45,000/MW for one that charges only from on-site solar.
The standalone premium comes at a price: cabling and grid fees of about €50,000/MW per year, against about €35,000/MW per year for the battery itself. It “costs more to pay the grid fees than to actually buy the batteries,” said Franceschino.
Pexapark’s Orlandi said “the most valuable asset has now become the grid connection point.” Utilities and traders still take almost all battery offtake, he said, although a handful of sophisticated German corporates have recently signed hybrid contracts.
The obstacle lies in where the money is. Half to two-thirds of a battery’s value comes from ancillary services, the balancing products that grid operators buy, Orlandi said, and most corporates have neither the interest nor the capability to trade them.
Risk allocation
Mathieu Ville, chief revenue officer at battery investor Tavion, questioned why sellers should accept zero-price floors. “Why would you floor me at zero? And if you do, why wouldn’t I cap you at 80?” he said. He was equally skeptical of
state-backed PPA guarantee schemes
. He said they look great “on paper” but have produced only three or four deals in five or six years, which he put down to their pricing and complexity.
Italy is about to test the model again. Francesca Morra, a partner at Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer in Milan, said the country’s energy regulator gave a positive opinion in October on rules for a new organized PPA market. The rules include a guarantee of last resort from GSE, the state-owned energy services company, which she said will be limited and fee-based to comply with EU state aid rules. Her advice was to settle key terms at the term-sheet stage. “The PPA is not an easy animal,” Morra said. “We need lawyers.”
But Ricardo Estévez Solís, senior originator at Centrica Energy, dismissed the idea that the market has stalled. He said that Spanish buyers facing forward prices above €100/MWh for next year are active alongside sellers, and that contracting is shifting from single assets to portfolios.
For large buyers, the question is now certainty. Cédric Saussez, head of green power structuring and origination for Northwestern Europe at
, said customers who once asked how green and how cheap a project was now ask how certain it is.
Rønnaug Sægrov Mysterud, head of energy sourcing at Norsk Hydro, said electricity makes up 30% to 40% of the cost of primary aluminum, leaving the company “extremely price sensitive.” Hydro needs sufficient power at competitive prices and certainty on indirect carbon cost compensation before it signs more PPAs, she said, adding that “the grid cost should not kill the rest.”
Carbon accounting
Carbon accounting rules are adding to the uncertainty. Daniela Fitzpatrick, senior manager energy procurement for Amazon Web Services, said up to 35% of renewable energy contracts globally could be stranded unless revisions to the GHG Protocol, the most widely used corporate carbon accounting standard, protect existing deals. “There’s a real concern that the draft GHG Protocol revisions are
cooling down the PPA market
,” said Fitzpatrick.
The rules may tighten further. Merve Güngör, policy and network manager for the RECS Energy Certificate Association, said the protocol’s standards board is weighing an age limit on eligible assets. “It’s not decided yet. I think 10 or 15 years are on the table,” said Güngör. A final standard is due at the end of 2028.
Javier de la Fuente Iglesias, head of flexibility and physical services at Statkraft, told
pv magazine
that industrial buyers see the value of battery arbitrage but do not yet know how to bring it into their procurement processes.
The premium buyers pay for firmer supply is already visible in pricing. LevelTen data for the second quarter put
hybrid solar-plus-storage PPAs
at a 24% premium to solar-only contracts.
