title: CGN connects first unit of world's highest-altitude CSP plant in Tibet - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Located at an altitude of 4,300 meters, the facility combines PV-powered molten salt heating, thermal energy storage and battery storage.
Vincent Shaw
09 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Utility-scale
The facility is part of a 150 MW demonstration project in Gar County that combines 100 MW of solar PV capacity with 50 MW of thermal power generation.
Chinese state-owned energy company
China General Nuclear Power Corp.
(CGN) connected the first 25 MW generating unit of its 50 MW concentrated solar power (CSP) plant in Tibet’s Ali Prefecture to the regional grid on Nov. 6. The company said the facility, located at an average elevation of 4,300 meters above sea level, is the world’s highest-altitude operational grid-connected CSP plant.
The facility is part of a 150 MW demonstration project in Gar County that combines 100 MW of solar PV capacity with 50 MW of CSP power generation. Total investment stands at approximately CNY 2.4 billion ($330 million). According to CGN, it is the first CSP project in Tibet to achieve grid connection.
The CSP installation consists of two 25 MW steam turbine units. The first was synchronized with the grid on Nov. 6, while the second is scheduled to come online by the end of 2026, bringing the facility to its full rated capacity.
Unlike conventional CSP plants, which use concentrated sunlight to generate heat, the Ali facility uses surplus PV electricity to power a molten salt electric heater with a peak rating of 205 MW. The system converts electricity into thermal energy for storage and subsequent power generation.
CGN said the project is the first CSP facility to integrate PV-powered electric heating, molten salt thermal storage and asynchronous battery storage. The company also claims that the 205 MW electric heater is the largest deployed in a CSP application worldwide. Neither claim, however, has been independently verified.
The plant incorporates a molten salt thermal storage system designed to provide 14 hours of storage, alongside a lithium-ion battery system for rapid frequency response. During the day, PV electricity generated independently of the grid powers the electric heater. Stored thermal energy is then used to drive the steam turbines at night or during periods of peak electricity demand.
The facility also operates as a combined heat and power plant, supplying district heating to Shiquanhe, the administrative center of Ali Prefecture, during the winter months.
CGN said the plant can switch between grid-connected and islanded operation, allowing it to supply electricity independently during grid disturbances. The capability is particularly relevant to Ali, a remote border region that has historically relied on diesel backup generation and electricity transmitted over long distances.
The company has also installed its proprietary distributed control system, which it said has been adapted to operate under the low atmospheric pressure and high ultraviolet radiation levels associated with the site’s elevation.
The project forms part of China’s efforts to expand CSP deployment. In late 2025, the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) and the National Energy Administration (NEA) jointly issued a policy directive targeting 15 GW of installed CSP capacity by 2030.
CGN also operates a 50 MW parabolic trough CSP plant in Delingha, Qinghai province. The facility recorded 2,824 equivalent full-load operating hours in 2024, the highest figure reported for a CSP plant in China that year.
The grid connection of the first unit marks an initial milestone for the high-altitude facility. However, the performance of its integrated PV-powered heating, thermal storage and cogeneration systems has yet to be demonstrated under sustained operating conditions, particularly during winter.

title: Massive solar project at Texas coal plant secures $1.8 billion green loan - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
The 1.2 GW Big Rooter Power solar project owned and funded by Panamint Capital will connect with the 342 MW Twin Oaks coal plant, creating a hybrid power station.
Anne Fischer
09 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
United States
Utility-scale
Construction on the first phase of the 1.2 GW Big Rooter Power solar project got underway in July at Panamint Capital’s Twin Oaks power station in Robertson County, Texas. The project will be the largest solar project constructed at an existing coal mining site and the largest brownfield renewable energy project in North America, according to Panamint.
The energy infrastructure investor recently closed on the first phase of a $1.8 billion green loan to finance construction. Proceeds from the $769 million first phase will fund ongoing construction of the 491 MW Big Rooter West portion of the project. The over $1 billion second phase of the Green Loan will finance construction of Big Rooter East, the project’s 658 MW second stage.
Located halfway between Dallas and Houston, Big Rooter Power is being built on 1,804 hectares of reclaimed coal mine land and operating interconnection infrastructure at Panamint’s 349 MW coal-fired Twin Oaks Complex. The campus combines power generation, surface mining, energy storage, data center capacity, and high voltage transmission.
“When Big Rooter is complete, the Twin Oaks complex will have 1.5 GW of operating thermal and renewable power, in addition to over 20 miles of new 345 kV transmission, 1.6 GWh of battery energy storage and 790 MW of Batch Zero data center capacity under development across our 10,000-acre site,” said Apolka Totth, Panamint’s chief executive officer.
Panamint reports it signed a long-term power purchase agreement (PPA) with an unnamed corporation. “Our long-term power purchase agreement with one of country’s largest companies will ensure the electricity we generate at Big Rooter will power job creation in the American economy into the 2050s,” said Bill Stanton, managing director of development at Panamint.
Construction of both Big Rooter West and Big Rooter East is expected to create over 800 jobs, Panamint reports.
Big Rooter East is the 658 MW second phase of the project and is slated to begin construction in December 2026 and enter commercial operation in August 2029. Financing on that phase is expected to close in Q1 2027.
Panamint reports it is committed to selecting domestic renewable energy companies. Solv Energy will provide EPC services for the project, including solar, substation and transmission infrastructure. First Solar will provide approximately 2 million solar panels manufactured in Ohio, Louisiana and Alabama. California-based Nextpower will deploy its NX Horizon solar tracker systems with Hail Pro-75 and NX Navigator software. In addition, the projects reportedly will use over 34,000 tons of domestically manufactured steel.
Nevada-based Panamint Capital is a woman-led energy investment company founded in 2019 thathad 718 MW of energy generating capacity in operation in 2025.
The company’s sustainability report points to the Twin Oaks station as an example of its redevelopment efforts that focus on preparing existing sites for utility-scale solar, storage and thermal projects. These projects, the report says, “extend the productive use of existing infrastructure through clean energy investments that support local employment and drive long-term economic value in the communities where we operate.”

content:
Markets & Policy
With the abolition of net metering just weeks away, households are increasingly turning to battery storage to protect the value of their solar energy. New figures from Sunergy Research reveal explosive growth across all battery categories, with plug-in batteries emerging as the market’s biggest breakthrough.
Emiliano Bellini
09 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Highlights
Residential
Sales of residential battery storage systems in the Netherlands have more than doubled over the past nine months ahead of the phaseout of the country’s net-metering scheme for residential PV at the end of this year, according to Sunergy Research, a Dutch energy supplier specializing in services for residential solar owners.
“Net metering will end on Jan. 1, and the market will change drastically for consumers,” Sunergy Research CEO Rolf Heynen told
ESS news
. “For many years, solar panels were easy to sell thanks to net metering and a very clear business case, with electricity prices stable at €0.21/kWh. Now, electricity prices have skyrocketed, and dynamic tariffs have made the business case more complex, alongside public discussions about the balancing market, variable grid tariffs starting in 2029, and home batteries.”
“With compensation for electricity exports expected to fall sharply, maximizing self-consumption is becoming increasingly important,” Heynen said. “Today, the average Dutch household consumes just 30% of the solar electricity it generates, exporting the remaining 70% to the grid. A home battery can dramatically reverse that balance, potentially increasing self-consumption to around 70%.”
Sunergy Research also reported that installations of small home batteries with capacities of up to 5 kWh were more than four times higher in September than in January, while installations of larger systems, ranging from 5 kWh to 15 kWh, nearly tripled over the same period.
The company’s data also show that installations of plug-in batteries, a relatively new segment of the Dutch energy storage market, have more than doubled in nine months, making them the largest category in the residential battery market.
Heynen said the rapid growth of plug-in batteries indicates that the market is expanding beyond early adopters.
“What makes this development particularly significant is the breadth of demand,” he said. “Smaller, accessible batteries are opening the market to ordinary households, while larger, permanently installed systems appeal to consumers who have already invested heavily in electrification. The barriers to battery ownership are falling rapidly.”
Sunergy has also launched its Home Batteries Selection Guide, a free, 33-page publication aimed at helping residential solar owners assess battery storage options.
The guide identifies two main market segments: plug-and-play batteries for smaller PV installations and permanently installed systems for households with higher electricity demand.
Plug-and-play batteries are particularly suitable for homes with around six solar panels and no heat pump or electric vehicle charger, according to the guide. These systems typically offer around 5 kWh of storage capacity, with prices starting at approximately €1,000 ($1,118.9).
Larger households may benefit from permanently installed batteries with capacities ranging from 5 kWh to 20 kWh, starting at approximately €4,000. The guide recommends capacities of 5 kWh to 10 kWh for typical single-phase installations and 10 kWh to 20 kWh for three-phase systems, depending on household requirements.
Battery sizing should take into account household electricity consumption, solar generation patterns, inverter capacity, backup power requirements and potential electricity trading, the report says. Sunergy also warns that oversized batteries are often recommended to consumers, potentially undermining investment returns.
Research estimates cited in the guide suggest payback periods of two to 15 years, with annual savings of approximately €200 to €1,000 for permanently installed systems. The guide also highlights the role of energy management systems (EMS) in coordinating solar generation, battery charging and household consumption.
The publication identifies additional revenue opportunities from electricity trading, grid balancing and congestion management. Sunergy also recommends professional installation, adequate ventilation and careful consideration of battery compatibility, expandability and insurance requirements.
The guide concludes that appropriately sized batteries combined with intelligent energy management could improve the economics of residential solar as the Netherlands phases out net metering.

title: Ecoprogetti presents automated line for recycling end-of-life PV modules - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The industrial line features a patented technology for the high-efficiency separation of glass from the solar panel, designed to maximise silicon recovery.
Patrick Jowett
09 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
Italian PV equipment manufacturer Ecoprogetti has delivered a fully-automated, industrial line for the recycling of end-of-life solar modules to Haiki+ Group, an Italian circular economy and environmental services company.
It has been operational since early 2025 in Sale, northwestern Italy, at a recycling and waste treatment plant. It is capable of processing up to 120 solar panels each hour, equivalent to approximately 4 tonnes an hour. This capacity corresponds to a nominal potential of around 700,000 tonnes annually if in continuous operation. It currently operates with an uptime of 94%, which Ecoprogetti says is one of the highest in the industry.
Ecoprogetti told
pv magazine
its line combines a patented air-based glass removal system with an electromechanical recycling process that separates module components through dedicated stages in order to minimise cross-contamination and preserve the quality of the recovered materials.
“The process includes automatic panel recognition, junction box and frame removal, module flipping, glass removal, material shredding, separation and collection,” the company explained.
Recovery results shared with
pv magazine
show conversion rates of 100% for aluminium and junction boxes, 99% for copper, glass and plastic and 95% for silicon at a purity of 100% for aluminium and junction boxes, 99% for glass, 98% for copper and silicon and 88% for plastic.
The line is capable of recycling mono and polycrystalline, double glass and bifacial solar panels, as well as the glass and backsheet from panels. It can also process modules with broken or cracked glass, missing parts, hail or fire damage, corrosion or delamination, as well as old or worn panels.
Ecoprogetti added that it is the only solution on the market capable of processing both conventional and double-glass PV modules using the same equipment, without requiring additional machinery or extra investment.
The company’s Managing Director Marco Manfron said the line demonstrates that photovoltaic recycling can be approached according to industrial principles of high capacity, automation, operational continuity and quality of the output material.
“The technology installed in Sale represents a tangible leap forward compared to previous solutions, because it makes it possible to process large volumes while reducing machine downtime and improving the quality of the recovered fractions,” Manfron said.
Ecoprogetti’s CEO Laura Sartore
recently spoke to
pv magazine
about the evolution of the global solar supply chain. The company
upgraded an existing PV module manufacturing line
in South Africa in August. It has also been expanding operations in the Middle East, most recently with
Iraq’s first solar module production line
and previously with
production lines in Oman

title: Panasonic releases new residential air-to-air heat pumps - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The reversible air-to-air heat pumps use R32 refrigerant and offer rated heating capacities ranging from 2.5 kW to 10.6 kW. Commercial availability in Japan is scheduled for January 2027.
Emiliano Bellini
09 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Heat pumps
Residential
The system’s outdoor unit
Japanese electronics manufacturer
Panasonic
has announced its new Eolia X Series of residential split air-to-air heat pumps, designed to provide space heating and cooling in Japanese homes.
Initially conceived for the Japanese market, new range comprises several capacity classes, with rated cooling outputs from 2.2 kW to 9.0 kW and rated heating outputs from 2.5 kW to 10.6 kW. Maximum heating capacity reaches 11.8 kW, depending on the model.
The systems use R32 (difluoromethane) refrigerant, with a global warming potential (GWP) of 675 and refrigerant charges ranging from 0.70 kg to 1.68 kg across the product lineup.
According to Panasonic’s published specifications, the units achieve annual performance factors (APF) of between 5.5 and 7.1 under the Japanese JIS C 9612:2013 standard. These values are not directly comparable with the seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP) figures commonly used for European heat pumps. However, they indicate relatively high seasonal efficiency, broadly consistent with modern high-efficiency inverter air-to-air heat pumps, which can achieve SCOP values of around 4 to 5.5 under European average-climate test conditions.
The company said the new generation features improvements to compressor operation during heating. Panasonic claims that the minimum heating output has been reduced by approximately 25% compared with a previous model, enabling more precise heating operation under low-load conditions.
The heat pumps comprise wall-mounted indoor units connected to outdoor units through refrigerant piping. Depending on the capacity class, the outdoor units measure 630 mm to 796 mm in height, 799 mm to 849 mm in width, and 299 mm to 319 mm in depth.
Panasonic also lists heating capacities at an outdoor temperature of 2 C ranging from 4.5 kW to 9.4 kW, depending on the model. The outdoor units incorporate corrosion-resistant components and coated electronic circuit boards.
Sales for the new Eolia X Series in Japan are expected to begin in late January 2027, the company said.

title: Solarwatt launches bifacial TOPCon solar module for BIPV applications - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
German solar manufacturer Solarwatt has added a new glass-glass module to its Construct series for building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV). The module features bifacial TOPCon cells, delivers up to 227 W/m² and has received general building approval in Germany.
Jochen Siemer
09 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
Residential
Solarwatt says its modules are particularly suitable for parking canopies.
German solar manufacturer Solarwatt has expanded its Construct series of building-integrated photovoltaic (BIPV) modules with the launch of the Panel vision M 5.0 construct. The Dresden-based company said the module has received general building authority approval, the so called allgemeine bauaufsichtliche Zulassung, or abZ, from the German Institute for Construction Technology (DIBt), joining several other products in its BIPV portfolio that have held the certification since 2020.
The approval simplifies regulatory procedures for applications that typically face more stringent building requirements, including overhead glazing and facade installations. Solarwatt said the new module is suitable for carports, parking canopies, facades and certain green roof applications.
“With our Construct modules, we significantly reduce the bureaucratic burden on contractors, as the abZ ensures that the primary regulatory hurdles have already been cleared,” said Solarwatt product manager Norbert Betzl. The certification provides architects, planners and installers with greater certainty when designing and implementing BIPV projects.
Solarwatt has not disclosed full technical specifications for the Panel vision M 5.0 construct. However, the company said the module uses bifacial tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) half-cut cells and delivers up to 227 W/m², representing an increase of more than 20% over the previous generation.
The new module features 3.2 mm-thick glass panes, compared with 2 mm glass in the Panel vision GM 3.0 construct. Solarwatt said the thicker glass, combined with a reinforced frame, improves resistance to high snow and wind loads, making the module suitable for applications in alpine regions and on high-rise facades. The company also claims high resistance to hail impacts.
Solarwatt said it has supplied modules with abZ certification for European projects totaling 33 MW since 2020.
The Panel vision M 5.0 construct is available to order through the Solarwatt Pro portal for installation partners. Like the company’s other glass-glass modules, it comes with a 30-year product warranty and a performance guarantee of at least 90% of its original rated output after 30 years.

title: Salt-based thermal storage supports renewable steam in Spain - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
A renewable steam project at Bayer’s pharmaceutical plant in Spain combines salt-based thermal storage with a 15 MW renewable power purchase agreement (PPA) and 2.5 MW of on-site solar, in an effort to replace fossil fuels used for industrial heat.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
09 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Energy Storage
German pharmaceutical company Bayer has begun testing a system that uses renewable electricity to produce steam at its plant in La Felguera, Langreo, in Spain’s Asturias region. The facility manufactures acetylsalicylic acid, the active ingredient in Aspirin. The project is designed to replace fossil fuels in steam generation.
Developed by Iberdrola España, the system combines a 15 MW renewable power purchase agreement, a 2.5 MW self-consumption solar installation and thermal energy storage using salt.
The storage system is intended to partially decouple electricity generation from the industrial process’s heat demand, helping maintain a continuous supply of steam. The project aims to meet 100% of the steam requirements for acetylsalicylic acid production with renewable electricity.
Testing began with the supply of renewable steam to the plant. The trial phase is expected to conclude by the end of the year, when the system is scheduled to reach continuous operation.
The project is structured around a long-term heat purchase agreement (HPA) and uses technology from Spanish engineering company Inerco to integrate the thermal storage system.
Iberdrola said the project represents an investment of more than €18 million. More than 60 professionals participated in the initial implementation phase.
The project has received public support from Spain’s Institute for Energy Diversification and Saving (IDAE) and Institute for Just Transition, as well as the regional government of Asturias and Langreo City Council. It has also received support from the European Union’s Innovation Fund.

title: Tongwei unveils 26.03%-efficient TOPCon solar cell with high sheet resistance - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
The solar cell was fabricated using a low-cost photoresist-based etching process to create a selective emitter with a sheet resistance of up to 1,600 Ω/sq in non-contacted regions, reducing recombination losses while maintaining effective electrical contacts. The TOPCon device achieved a certified power conversion efficiency of 26.03% and an open-circuit voltage of 746.5 mV.
Emiliano Bellini
09 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
A research group led by Chinese polysilicon and solar module manufacturer
has developed a tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) solar cell featuring an emitter with higher sheet resistance in a bid to reduce recombination losses, improve surface passivation and increase power conversion efficiency.
“In our work, a non-destructive photoresist-based etching process was used to form a selective emitter structure for TOPCon solar cells,” corresponding author Xiajie Meng told
pv magazine
. “The structure features a sheet resistance as high as 1,600 Ω/sq – to the best of our knowledge, the highest reported for TOPCon to date. This successful implementation confirms that TOPCon remains highly competitive for commercial applications.”
The researchers explained that conventional TOPCon cells face a trade-off between low contact resistance and reduced carrier recombination in the boron-doped emitter. The proposed architecture addresses this limitation by combining heavily boron-doped regions beneath the metal contacts with lightly doped regions between the contacts.
The scientists used a range of characterization techniques to investigate the structural, electrical and passivation properties of the proposed cell architecture, with the aim of identifying optimal design conditions that balance surface passivation, lateral charge transport and metal shading losses.
They used scanning electron microscopy and 3D laser microscopy to examine etching depth and surface morphology, while four-point probe measurements determined the sheet resistance of the lightly and heavily boron-doped emitter regions. They also evaluated contact resistivity using the transmission line method and characterized doping profiles and junction depths through electrochemical capacitance-voltage measurements.
The team assessed minority carrier lifetime and emitter recombination using quasi-steady-state photoconductance measurements. Electron-beam-induced current measurements provided qualitative evidence of junction continuity, while photoluminescence imaging was used to evaluate passivation quality under different illumination levels.
Current-voltage measurements were used to determine key cell parameters, including open-circuit voltage, short-circuit current density, fill factor, efficiency and series resistance. The researchers also conducted Quokka3 simulations to compare conventional uniform emitters, selective emitters and locally boron-doped finger structures using experimentally derived parameters.
The analysis showed that that high-temperature oxidation reduced surface boron concentrations while increasing junction depth, helping suppress recombination and maintain effective metal contacts.
The scientists also found that increasing the sheet resistance of non-contacted emitter regions from 800 Ω/sq to 2,000 Ω/sq significantly improved minority carrier lifetime and surface passivation, although improvements became marginal beyond 1,600 Ω/sq, while doping uniformity deteriorated, making this value preferable for cell fabrication.
The team then compared three architectures: a conventional uniform emitter, a boron-doped selective emitter and a locally boron-doped finger structure. The selective emitter combined a sheet resistance of 450 Ω/sq beneath the metal contacts with 1,600 Ω/sq in non-contacted regions.
This configuration increased average cell efficiency from 25.82% to 25.98%, representing an absolute improvement of 0.16 percentage points.
Open-circuit voltage increased from 742.6 mV to 745.5 mV, while fill factor improved from 83.54% to 83.76%.
The optimized selective emitter cell also achieved a certified efficiency of 26.03%, with an open-circuit voltage of 746.5 mV, with the results being confirmed by Germany’s
Solar Energy Research Hamelin
(ISFH). The locally boron-doped finger structure also improved passivation but suffered greater fill factor losses, limiting its efficiency advantage. Its fill factor reached 83.34%, compared with 83.76% for the selective emitter, partly reflecting increased series resistance and potentially additional recombination.
The Quokka3 simulations examined the effects of contact width, grid pitch, finger width and wafer resistivity on cell performance and indicated that a contacted-region width of approximately 200 µm offered the highest efficiency among the investigated configurations. Reducing metal finger widths to 7 µm to 9 µm could enable a denser grid with a pitch of around 500 µm to 550 µm, potentially improving efficiency further, the scientists said.
“For the locally boron-doped finger architecture, simulations indicate that using silicon wafers with higher bulk resistivity alongside more closely spaced front contacts could offer opportunities for further performance improvements, although experimental validation is still required,” Meng stated. “More broadly, the study demonstrates the potential of photoresist-based selective etching to produce emitters with exceptionally high sheet resistance in non-contacted areas without compromising electrical contact quality.”
The new cell concept was described in “
High-efficiency TOPCon solar cells featuring super-high sheet resistance emitters via low-cost photoresist etching
,” which was recently published in
Solar Energy Materials and Solar Cells
. The research team included scientists from the School of Optoelectronic Science and Engineering, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China (UESTC) and Chinese industrial equipment company Jiangsu Inspiray Equipment Co., Ltd.
“The findings could help manufacturers refine emitter doping profiles and contact designs, paving the way for further efficiency gains and potential industrial adoption of the technology,” Meng concluded.

title: New wheeled factory robot works alongside humans without safety cages
content: Swiss startup Embodied AI has unveiled AIR, a two-armed mobile robot designed to work alongside factory employees without requiring a safety cage. The company said AIR initially operates under remote supervision before learning to perform assigned tasks independently within about a month. Embodied AI reported an average task success rate of 95 percent across paid manufacturing pilots, including deployments with companies in the consumer electronics and automotive sectors.“Safety and reliability are non-negotiable requirements of physical AI to enter the real world at scale. These are the principles that guided the design of AIR,” said Francesco Stella, co-founder and CEO of Embodied AI, in a statement. Tendon-driven humanoidAIR is a two-armed mobile robot designed to perform manufacturing tasks alongside factory workers without requiring a conventional safety cage.Developed by a 25-person team spun out of the Swiss technical university EPFL, the robot combines a torso, two lightweight arms, and a wheeled base. Unlike conventional industrial robots that rely on rigid structures and external safety barriers, AIR uses a compliant mechanical design intended to reduce the risk of injury during accidental contact.The robot’s architecture centers on keeping heavy components inside its torso while using a tendon-driven mechanism to operate its arms. Cables transmit movement from the motors to the arms, reducing the mass of the moving components. This arrangement allows the arms to remain lightweight and give way when they encounter an obstacle or make contact with a person.The design is intended to address a major limitation of conventional factory automation. Industrial robotic arms are often heavy and rigid, making them difficult to deploy in workspaces shared directly with people. As a result, many installations require physical barriers or light curtains to separate machines from employees. AIR instead relies on mechanical compliance and a mass distribution that keeps heavier components away from the robot’s moving limbs.The only specific mechanical figures disclosed so far concern the arm. According to an investor description, the tendon-driven unit weighs approximately 2 kilograms (4.4 pounds) and can lift to 5 kilograms (11 pounds). The company has not yet published AIR’s overall dimensions, weight, reach, battery capacity, or maximum payload.Another central feature is its approach to learning manufacturing tasks. AIR initially operates through teleoperation, with a remote human operator controlling the robot during its first shifts. These operations generate training data that the company’s AI system uses to learn the assigned task. Embodied AI says the robot can transition to autonomous operation within approximately one month, allowing it to take over work that initially required human supervision.Targets factory automationThe company is not starting with an entirely untested software platform. AIR uses the same AI stack already deployed in a two-armed robotic cell operating on a customer’s production line. The company has used this system in paid manufacturing pilots with a consumer electronics manufacturer and an automotive and industrial technology supplier.Embodied AI reported that an average task success rate of 95 percent across these deployments. However, it has not disclosed how many tasks it evaluated, how long the trials ran, or how it calculated the success rate. The company also said that, depending on the application, a single AIR unit could handle workloads equivalent to as many as three workers per shift.The robot’s initial deployment model combines human supervision with progressive automation rather than requiring complete autonomy before entering a factory. This allows manufacturers to use the machine for productive work while its AI system gathers operational data. The approach also gives the company an opportunity to refine task-specific capabilities using information collected in actual manufacturing environments rather than relying exclusively on laboratory demonstrations.Although it is described as a humanoid, AIR does not have legs or a bipedal walking system. Its wheeled platform provides mobility around factory workspaces, while its upper body and two arms allow it to interact with equipment and handle objects. This configuration places it closer to a class of mobile manipulation robots designed for industrial applications than to full-size, legged humanoids.The company has not disclosed a price or delivery schedule, but says it will begin accepting orders following the robot’s unveiling at Humanoid Europe 2026 in Munich.

title: Nvidia opens probe as CEO admits involvement with suspect Chinese spy
content: Nvidia has launched an independent investigation after reports that chief executive Jensen Huang was targeted by an alleged Chinese intelligence operative. The inquiry is expected to examine internal communications and access protocols. However, the board stated it has “no reason to believe” that any designs or national security were compromised.The move follows reporting by The New York Times. According to the report, US intelligence agencies identified Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang as an operative for Beijing during her relationship with the Nvidia chief.Outside legal counsel will assist a committee of independent directors to evaluate all available records. The board said its primary focus remains the integrity of Nvidia’s technical assets and broader American economic security.“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” remarked the board in an official statement.Executive memo addressing inquiry cooperationAlongside the security review, Mr Huang issued an internal memo to staff acknowledging an extramarital relationship. In the note, he apologized to his family, colleagues, and investors for personal conduct that fell short of his responsibilities.He also addressed the counterintelligence reports directly. Mr Huang stated that he is cooperating fully with the independent inquiry, affirming his commitment to protect company secrets and support federal national security standards.“Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation,” noted Huang. “I support the investigation and will cooperate fully.”Nvidia’s board confirmed that Mr Huang retains its confidence and will continue to lead the company. The board noted that further operational updates will follow once the committee completes its assessment.Delicate time for NvidiaThe investigation comes at a delicate time for Nvidia. The firm designs the specialized graphics processors that are highly required for modern artificial intelligence, from enterprise data centers run by Microsoft and Google to frontier research labs. That market dominance has turned the company into a critical piece of American technological infrastructure.For foreign intelligence services, gaining visibility into Nvidia’s hardware roadmap, advanced packaging methods, or executive decision-making would represent a major strategic breakthrough.The inquiry also lands amid intense geopolitical pressure. The US Department of Commerce has spent the past several years tightening export curbs on advanced computing hardware to restrict China’s access to cutting-edge silicon.Lawmakers and federal regulators closely track compliance across the semiconductor supply chain. Because Huang is the public face of Nvidia and directs its engineering strategy, any foreign intelligence contact touching his inner circle is certain to draw scrutiny from US defense officials.For the board, the primary task is proving that corporate networks, hardware blueprints, and sensitive partner discussions remained secure. Outside investigators may examine Huang’s official correspondence, travel schedules, and personal device usage alongside company access logs.Technical audits might focus on whether any product specifications, agreements, or software libraries were exposed during the relationship. Nvidia indicated that the committee will share its findings once the review concludes.

title: China’s bubble-lubrication system cuts cargo ships energy use by 5%
content: Chinese engineers have adapted a drag-reduction principle associated with high-speed underwater projectiles to improve the energy efficiency of commercial ships. A second-generation bubble-lubrication system installed on a newly built 50,000-tonne product and chemical tanker reportedly reduced net energy consumption by about 5% during a five-month operational trial.Developed by the Shanghai Merchant Ship Design and Research Institute, the system injects compressed air beneath a vessel’s hull to create a layer of bubbles that reduces friction with the surrounding water. The tanker has entered service, and the results suggest the technology could help shipping operators lower fuel consumption without changing their vessels’ primary propulsion systems. Furthermore, the institute estimates that a 5% reduction could save roughly one metric ton of fuel per day on a tanker of this size.Bubble lubrication reduces friction beneath the hullThe technology draws on the broader principle of reducing contact between an object and surrounding water. Supercavitating torpedoes, for example, travel inside a gas-filled cavity that substantially reduces their contact with water, allowing them to reach extremely high underwater speeds.The commercial shipping system uses a different implementation of the underlying idea. Rather than creating a large cavity around a fast-moving projectile, it continuously injects compressed air beneath the ship’s hull, forming a layer of microbubbles between the hull and seawater, the South China Morning Post reported.This changes the flow of water close to the vessel’s surface, creating a gas-liquid mixture that reduces frictional resistance. With less resistance to overcome, the ship can require less propulsion power to maintain its speed.The overall efficiency gains depend on the balance between the power saved through reduced hull friction and the electricity consumed by the compressors supplying the air. The reported 5% net energy saving accounts for that additional energy demand, although the institute has not provided a detailed breakdown of the trial results.Automated controls improve the second-generation systemThe second-generation Bubble Lubrication System builds on an earlier version tested aboard a 1,800-TEU feeder container ship in April 2022. Development of the upgraded system began the following month, with engineers seeking to address the earlier design’s reliance on manual operation.The new version includes an improved air-supply structure intended to reduce compressor power consumption, alongside automated controls and monitoring capabilities. Its intelligent control system adjusts the volume of air supplied beneath the hull according to the vessel’s speed and draught.A digital operational support system also monitors and analyses energy efficiency in real time. These functions are intended to make the technology easier to operate across changing sailing conditions, while reducing the energy required to generate the bubbles.The system is designed to work with different commercial vessel types and propulsion technologies. According to the institute, it is compatible with ships powered by LNG, electricity, methanol and ammonia. The new developments provide an additional basis for its deployment on commercial vessels, although wider adoption will depend on performance across different hull designs, operating conditions and routes.

title: US' largest underwater stealth logistics fleet to be built with new funding
content: A defense technology startup is set to transform undersea logistics with ultra-large autonomous underwater vehicles designed to transport critical payloads across contested maritime environments.Corridian, a New England-based defence technology startup, has emerged from stealth with a $38 million seed funding round to accelerate the development of its ultra-large Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs). The funding round was led by Point72 Ventures, with participation from Balerion Space Ventures, Harpoon Ventures, DCVC, Marlinspike, and several additional defence and deep-tech investors.Autonomous underwater vehicles manufacturingThe company also highlighted that inexpensive drones and long-range missiles have made ships and aircraft easier to find and costlier to defend, leaving the military with few survivable ways to move payloads and materiel across contested waters. At the same time, the Navy’s undersea payload capacity is limited to existing AUV and submarine platforms, which were not designed to carry large, numerous, or dense payloads. As a result, the United States and allied nations must close a widening gap in their ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities across contested regions, such as those in the Western Pacific.“America’s dependence on the surface and air domains to move mass at scale is an acute vulnerability,” said Mike Guay, co-founder and CEO of Corridian. “The United States and its allies are buying drones, sensors, effects, and supplies that need a way to reach the fight, even when operating in heavily contested and denied environments. That’s stealth logistics: carrying that cargo underwater, out of sight, autonomously, thousands of nautical miles at a time. Corridian adds the undersea capacity commanders need, working alongside the submarines that operate at the tip of the spear today.”Corridian designs its platforms to carry ISO-standard, containerized payloads across vast distances, traveling thousands of nautical miles without a crew, stealthily and with high survivability. Corridian draws on a supply chain that is independent of the Submarine Industrial Base, adding capacity without competing for the shipyards and suppliers that build crewed submarines. Its initial capabilities focus on payload and effects delivery; intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance; and contested logistics. The company plans to unveil its flagship vehicle in 2027, according to a press release.Undersea technologies“We are excited by the commitment the U.S. Navy has shown to the undersea domain, and we see an opportunity in that space for larger AUVs that can deliver greater payload capacity and range at a lower cost,” said Chris Morales, Partner at Point72 Ventures and former naval officer. “We believe the Corridian founders have the knowledge and experience needed to pursue this opportunity, from a deep understanding of undersea technologies to a history of delivering high-impact Navy programs of record. We’re thrilled to back them as they take on this highly ambitious and timely work.”Developing ultra-large autonomous underwater vehicles involves significant engineering challenges, including navigation, endurance, communications, payload integration, manufacturing, and operational reliability. The company’s planned 2027 unveiling of its flagship vehicle will be an important milestone in demonstrating its technological progress and long-term ambitions.“The character of war is changing, and the force that adapts first will have the advantage,” said retired Adm. Lisa Franchetti, 33rd Chief of Naval Operations and senior military advisor to Corridian. “AUVs are a critical part of the solution, but only if they can operate at scale, with the ranges and payloads the theater actually demands. Corridian is addressing a real operational gap in a way that is both technically credible and scalable. The team understands both the mission and how to execute it.”

title: Anti-submarine warfare gets major boost as hybrid fleet vision advances
content: A French company has taken a significant step to strengthen its anti-submarine warfare. Thales is enabling navies to achieve superior underwater awareness and operational advantage through hybrid fleets and manned-unmanned teaming.Through its Hybrid Fleet vision, Thales is enabling navies to move beyond traditional platform-centric operations towards a connected, scalable and resilient ASW ecosystem.At Euronaval 2026, Thales highlighted three major technological developments supporting this vision — the M-Cube mission management system, a new Lightweight Dipping Sonar (LDS), and the CAPTAS-4 Mission Module (C4MM). These technologies intended to create flexible anti-submarine warfare architectureTogether, these technologies are intended to create a connected and flexible anti-submarine warfare architecture, enabling navies to distribute sensors across multiple platforms and coordinate their activities through an integrated operational environment.“The future of Anti-Submarine Warfare is not about a single platform. It is about the ability to connect ships, autonomous systems and advanced sensors into a coordinated operational ecosystem,” said Sébastien Guérémy, Vice-President, UnderWater Systems, Thales. “Through these technologies, Thales is helping navies maintain decisive advantage in an increasingly contested underwater environment.”At the heart of Thales’ Hybrid Fleet vision is M-Cube, which provides the mission management and command-and-control framework required to coordinate complex operations involving crewed and uncrewed platforms.Designed to support collaborative operationsDesigned to support collaborative operations across multiple domains, M-Cube enables operators to plan, task and supervise distributed assets from a single mission environment. By orchestrating the deployment of ships, helicopters, unmanned surface vessels and other autonomous systems, it allows navies to conduct coordinated ASW operations over wider areas with increased operational efficiency and responsiveness, according to a press release.Originally developed and proven in mine warfare missions, M-Cube is now expanding to Anti-Submarine Warfare, ISR and Above Water Warfare applications, providing a scalable and interoperable architecture aligned with NATO operational requirements, as per the release. The company revealed that the Hybrid Fleet vision also relies on multiplying the number of sensors available within the battlespace. To address this challenge, Thales is introducing its Lightweight Dipping Sonar (LDS).Derived from decades of expertise in advanced sonar technologies, LDS extends high-performance acoustic detection capabilities to a new generation of autonomous and lightweight platforms. Compact, modular and highly deployable, the system enables unmanned vessels and other non-traditional platforms to perform sophisticated underwater surveillance and submarine detection missions. By allowing advanced sonar capabilities to be deployed further forward and for extended periods of time, LDS significantly enhances operational persistence while reducing risks to personnel and high-value assets, as per the release. Complementing this distributed architecture is the CAPTAS-4 Mission Module, which brings the proven performance of the world-leading CAPTAS-4 variable-depth sonar to a wider range of naval platforms. Packaged as a modular, deployable and cross-deckable capability, it offers maximum operational flexibility across heterogeneous fleet. The CAPTAS-4 Mission Module enables navies to rapidly equip vessels with high-end ASW capabilities without requiring dedicated ASW frigates. This unprecedented flexibility allows operators to adapt their force structure to mission requirements while maintaining the level of performance needed to detect and track increasingly silent submarine threats, according to Thales.By extending advanced underwater warfare capabilities across a broader fleet, CAPTAS-4 Mission Module plays a key role in enabling distributed and scalable ASW operations.

title: Physicists build three-flavor quantum system to probe competing forces
content: What happens when three different kinds of particles interact, and each pair behaves differently?Physicists have now recreated this situation in the laboratory, building a three-component quantum system that displays competing magnetic correlations.The achievement could help investigate some of physics’ hardest problems, including high-temperature superconductivity and the interactions governing particles inside atomic nuclei.How researchers built a three-component quantum systemThe traditional Hubbard model describes interacting electrons using two possible spin states: spin-up and spin-down. Despite its relatively simple mathematical structure, it remains notoriously difficult to solve.Adding a third component could reveal new quantum behaviors, but three-body collisions can cause atoms to disappear from the system, making experiments difficult to sustain.A team of international researchers overcame this challenge using ultracold lithium-6 atoms. The researchers placed them in an optical lattice, an artificial crystal created with laser light that provides regularly spaced positions for atoms.The atoms can tunnel between neighboring sites, effectively moving from one position to another. Instead of using two, the team employed three different internal quantum states of lithium-6 to represent distinct fermionic components.By adjusting the magnetic field, they could independently tune the interactions between each pair, giving them control over three different interaction strengths.Watching competing quantum behaviorsTo observe these interactions, the researchers developed a flavor-resolved quantum gas microscope that could distinguish the three components and locate individual atoms. This allowed them to examine how the particles occupied lattice sites and interacted.One important target was a Mott insulating state, in which strong interactions suppress multiple occupancy of lattice sites and restrict particle movement. The researchers identified this behavior by measuring fluctuations in atomic occupancy and the system’s response to changes in density.“It was particularly important to us to observe a so-called Mott state, in which the interactions suppress the double occupation of sites,” Peter Schauss, one of the study authors and a physics professor at the University of Virginia, said.The experiment revealed competing quantum behaviors. Depending on interaction strengths, some pairs of components displayed ferromagnetic correlations, while others showed antiferromagnetic correlations.The researchers also measured triply occupied sites, where all three components shared a location. These measurements agreed with numerical calculations performed by collaborators at Rice University.A three-flavor system could bring quark physics into the labThe findings could help physicists investigate questions that conventional calculations have struggled to answer. Kaden Hazzard, a Rice University associate professor and co-author, explained:“Although the Hubbard model is important and simple to write down, it isn’t easy to solve. Theorists have been banging our heads on the two-component Hubbard model for decades, yet there are still major open questions. Adding a third tunable component lets us see how the two-component model reacts to it, potentially helping us answer these major questions,”He also highlighted the relationship between experiments and theoretical research:“The experiments are a wonderful testing ground for theoretical ideas. Sohail and I were able to compare sophisticated numerical calculations to the experiments, which are already pushed to the boundaries of our capabilities. These comparisons will feed back into helping us refine our theoretical tools. It’s an exciting and fast-developing time.”Three-body collisions still cause atom losses, while heating makes it difficult to reach the low temperatures needed to explore more delicate quantum phases. Nevertheless, the system proved surprisingly stable\“It turned out that the experimental realization is surprisingly stable,” Schauss said. “Usually, one fears that three-body collisions could quickly destroy the system. Despite this potential danger, we were able to successfully carry out the measurements and observe a Mott insulator,” Schauss said:The researchers plan to refine the interactions, investigate a possible paired Mott state and explore triangular and kagome lattices. Ultimately, the system could help simulate aspects of quantum chromodynamics, which describes interactions between quarks inside protons and neutrons.Its three components resemble the three color charges of quarks, while the platform could also shed light on interactions behind high-temperature superconductivity.The study is published in the journal Science.

title: A surprise 15,000-pound right whale calf is this season’s 24th birth
content: Scientists spotted a surprise North Atlantic right whale calf in Canadian waters. They say the discovery is a cause for celebration.The discovery comes as the critically endangered species continues to face threats from fishing-gear entanglements and vessel strikes. The aquarium estimates that around 380 North Atlantic right whales remain.On September 25, researchers with the Mingan Island Cetacean Study photographed a mother and calf near Anticosti Island, Quebec, according to the New England Aquarium’s press release.The photographs were sent to scientists at the aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center for Ocean Life, which manages the North Atlantic Right Whale Catalog, a database used to identify and track individual whales.After weeks of comparing photographs and examining sighting records, researchers determined that the calf was new. The calf’s mother was identified as Silt, Catalog #1817, a whale at least 38 years old that has now given birth to six known calves.Silt had not been seen since February. She avoided detection during boat-based and aerial surveys along the U.S. East Coast throughout the spring and summer.“This is an exciting discovery for us so late in the year,” said Amy Warren, a scientist at the aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center, in the news release.The new calf, estimated at about 15,000 pounds (6,804 kilograms), was identified more than five months after the annual calving season ended, which runs from mid-November through mid-April in the southeastern United States.Researchers initially documented 23 mother-calf pairs. This surprising discovery off Quebec has increased that total to 24.A family marked by survival and lossSilt has had six known calves, three grandchildren, and one great-grandchild, born in 2026.The aquarium reported that Silt has survived at least five fishing-gear entanglements, some of which left substantial scarring on her head and tail. Two of her offspring died following these encounters. Division, born in 2022, died this year following a severe entanglement. Her oldest known calf passed away in 2005 after being struck by a vessel. That family history shows the dangers this species faces in the North Atlantic. Researchers hope Silt’s newest calf will not face the same threats. On a hopeful notePhys.org described 2025-2026 as the most productive calving season since 2009. The recently discovered calf was welcomed as hopeful news as the species population remains small.Only about 70 reproductive-age females remain. The species lost about 25 percent of its population between 2010 and 2020. No calves were born in 2018. The population has recovered somewhat since 2020, but right whales still face threats.The New England Aquarium maintains the North Atlantic Right Whale Catalog in collaboration with researchers and organizations along the eastern seaboard of North America and eastern Canada.According to the news release, the catalog documents births, injuries, migration patterns, and ages. Scientists reconstruct individual whales’ histories. However, Silt’s newest calf demonstrates that even extensive surveys can miss individual animals.“It just goes to show you how big the ocean is, and how those animals can get lost out there,” Sears said in Phys. The latest sighting adds another calf to one of the strongest breeding seasons recorded for North Atlantic right whales. It is a promising development for the species.

title: B-2 vs B-21: What makes America's new stealth bomber different?
content: For more than two decades, the B-2 Spirit has represented the cutting edge of American stealth-bomber technology. Its distinctive flying-wing design, long range, and ability to carry conventional and nuclear weapons made it one of the most capable aircraft in the US military. Now, its successor, the B-21 Raider, is preparing to take over that role with a design intended for an increasingly contested battlefield.Developed by Northrop Grumman for the US Air Force, the B-21 is not simply a newer version of the B-2. It introduces advances in stealth, networking, computing, and maintainability, reflecting how long-range air combat has evolved since the Spirit first entered service in the 1990s.From the B-2 Spirit to the B-21 RaiderThe B-2 was developed during the Cold War to penetrate heavily defended Soviet airspace and strike strategic targets without being detected by radar. It first flew in July 1989 and entered operational service in 1997.Its flying-wing configuration, composite material, and radar-absorbing coatings help reduce its radar signature. Four General Electric F118 engines power the aircraft, which has a 172-foot (52-meter) wingspan, an unrefueled range of about 6,000 nautical miles, and a maximum weapons payload of 60,000 pounds (27,216 kilograms).The bomber can carry both conventional and nuclear weapons, including precision-guided munitions and the massive GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator. In June 2025, B-2s used the 30,000-pound bunker-busting weapon during Operation Midnight Hammer against Iranian nuclear facilities.However, the B-2’s advanced design comes with significant maintenance demands. Its low-observable coatings and specialized structures require careful inspection and restoration to preserve its stealth characteristics. Keeping the aircraft mission-ready has therefore remained a major challenge for the Air Force.The B-21 is intended to address these requirements while introducing a more adaptable platform for future operations.What makes the B-21 different?Like the B-2, the B-21 uses a flying-wing configuration and carries its weapons internally to reduce its radar signature. However, the Raider incorporates advances in low-observable materials, propulsion integration, and digital engineering developed over several decades.The Air Force describes it as a dual-capable penetrating strike bomber, designed to deliver conventional and nuclear weapons against heavily defended targets. Unlike the B-2, the Raider is also being developed around an open systems architecture.This lets engineers update software, integrate new sensors, and add weapons with less reliance on redesigning the entire aircraft. The approach is intended to help the bomber adapt as radar systems, electronic warfare capabilities, and other air-defense technologies evolve.The B-21 will also operate as part of a broader family of systems involving intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, electronic attack, communications and other capabilities. Rather than functioning solely as an independent strike aircraft, it is designed to exchange information with other platforms and contribute to a connected battlespace.Many of its specifications remain classified. The Air Force has not publicly disclosed its exact range, speed, payload capacity, or radar signature, making direct performance comparisons with the B-2 difficult.A different approach to operating costs and productionThe B-21 is also designed for long-term maintenance and affordability. Its newer materials and manufacturing methods are intended to reduce the time and resources required to maintain its low-observable characteristics.The Air Force lists an average procurement unit cost of $692 million in fiscal year 2022 dollars, based on a planned minimum fleet of 100 aircraft. This figure includes procurement-related costs and should not be compared directly with the B-2’s historical unit cost, which was calculated using a different accounting basis.The service currently plans to acquire at least 100 Raiders, although senior military officials have discussed the possibility of a larger fleet. As of 2026, the B-21 remains in flight testing. The aircraft has demonstrated aerial refueling with a KC-135 Stratotanker, an important milestone for its long-range mission profile. The Air Force is targeting the arrival of its first operational aircraft at Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota in 2027. Production capacity has also been expanded by 25% to accelerate deliveries.Why the B-2 will still remain relevantThe introduction of the B-21 does not mean the B-2 will disappear immediately. The Air Force continues to invest in upgrades, maintenance, and low-observable improvements to keep the existing fleet operational until its successor is ready.The two aircraft represent different stages in the evolution of stealth aviation. The B-2 demonstrated that a large strategic bomber could penetrate sophisticated air defenses using low-observable design. The B-21 builds on that foundation with more adaptable software, advanced networking, and an emphasis on sustained operations.Raider’s significance will depend not just on how difficult it is to detect, but on how effectively it can operate alongside other military systems and adapt to changing threats. As the US Air Force prepares to introduce the B-21, the transition is a shift from the pioneering stealth technology of the Cold War toward a more connected and digitally adaptable generation of long-range strike aircraft.

title: A Monster Solar Storm Turned a Protected Region Around Earth Into a Particle Accelerator
content:
Ultrarelativistic electrons in an impenetrable barrier following a solar superstorm. Credit: Miyoshi et al., Geophysical Research Letters 2026
A solar superstorm appears to have turned a normally sheltered region near Earth into a natural particle accelerator, boosting electrons to energies capable of penetrating some satellite shielding.
Protecting spacecraft from radiation means understanding where hazardous particles can appear, especially during severe solar storms. Near Earth, an invisible boundary was thought to keep exceptionally energetic electrons out of a relatively protected region. During and after the geomagnetic superstorm of May 2024, Japan’s Arase space probe, operated by JAXA, detected large numbers of them well inside it. Some had energies exceeding three megaelectronvolts, enough to pass through some satellite shielding.
Researchers led by Nagoya University analyzed Arase’s observations to determine how these electrons appeared in a region that normally excludes them. Their evidence suggests the particles gained energy there, rather than entering it already highly energized. The distinction matters because it means a radiation hazard can develop within the supposedly protected region itself.
An electron barrier with uncertain origins
Earth’s magnetic field traps charged particles, including protons and electrons, in two doughnut-shaped regions called the Van Allen radiation belts. These particles can damage the hardware and electronics of spacecraft passing through the belts. At the inner edge of the outer belt, roughly three times Earth’s radius from the planet’s center, the most energetic electrons usually seem to encounter an invisible wall. Under typical conditions, the region inside this boundary is devoid of these extremely fast-moving electrons.
Detailed schematic outlining the process of electron acceleration inside the impenetrable barrier. Credit: Miyoshi et al, Geophysical Research Letters, 2026
Scientists first identified the apparent barrier in 2014, but its origin remains incompletely understood. One possible explanation involves “plasmaspheric hiss,” low-frequency radio waves that sound like static when played through a speaker. These waves occur in Earth’s magnetosphere, the region of space dominated by its magnetic field. Human-made very-low-frequency radio transmissions used to communicate with submarines underwater may also help shape the boundary by scattering radiation-belt electrons into Earth’s atmosphere.
“One of the key questions was how these highly energetic electrons appeared inside the barrier,” said Yoshizumi Miyoshi, a professor at the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research (ISEE) at Nagoya University and the study’s lead author. “Were they transported inward from the outer radiation belt, or were they accelerated locally within this region?”
Chirping waves may accelerate electrons for days
The intense solar activity behind the May 2024 superstorm brought northern lights to Hokkaido and as far south as Japan’s Hyogo prefecture. In space, the storm dramatically eroded Earth’s plasmasphere, a region filled with relatively cool charged particles. Its outer boundary retreated unusually close to the planet, leaving the area around the usual electron barrier much less densely populated with plasma. Hotter electrons could then reach farther inward and generate natural, low-frequency electromagnetic waves known as chorus waves.
Arase detected intense chorus waves repeatedly sweeping upward in frequency. “When converted into audio, it sounds like a bird song,” Miyoshi said. These waves ripple through Earth’s magnetic field and can transfer energy to electrons when their oscillations match the electrons’ spiraling motion around magnetic field lines.
“Typically, the plasmasphere recovers on a timescale of about two days,” Miyoshi said. “During the May 2024 superstorm, however, it took approximately 4.3 to 4.7 days for the plasma density to recover to more than half of its pre-storm level in the observed region.”
The resulting low-density conditions persisted for several days, potentially allowing chorus-wave activity and the continued acceleration of electrons inside the previously impenetrable barrier.
Chorus waves rising in frequency recorded by Arase in March 2018 converted into audio. Credit: Erg Science Center
Evidence of acceleration within the barrier
To distinguish local acceleration from the inward movement of already energetic electrons, the researchers analyzed electron phase space density, or PSD. This quantity describes how electrons are distributed according to their energies and motion. Using measurements from multiple Arase orbits, the team examined how PSD varied with distance from Earth while accounting for changes in the electrons’ motion.
A distinct local peak developed near the usual barrier boundary and grew stronger over time. That growing peak provided evidence that electrons were gaining energy within the region, rather than simply being transported inward from the outer radiation belt.
Miyoshi said the findings, published in
Geophysical Research Letters
, show that even parts of near-Earth space considered relatively protected from extremely energetic electrons can experience substantial increases in radiation during severe space weather. The observations also offer insight into how Earth’s magnetosphere responds to extreme solar activity and underscore the value of continuously monitoring the space environment around the planet.
“This discovery highlights the need to understand and predict how energetic electrons behave under extreme space weather conditions,” Miyoshi said. “Such knowledge is important for assessing radiation risks to spacecraft and improving future space weather predictions.”

title: The Solar System May Have a 6th Dwarf Planet – and It’s Been Hiding in Plain Sight
content:
Artist’s concept of a dwarf planet. Astronomers have discovered a remarkably large icy object beyond Pluto that could become the solar system’s sixth officially recognized dwarf planet. Credit: SciTechDaily.com
A newly discovered dwarf planet candidate has a trail stretching back more than a decade in telescope images, giving astronomers a head start in understanding its orbit.
2026 ED138 could become the solar system’s sixth officially recognized dwarf planet. The newly discovered icy body orbits beyond Pluto, and early measurements suggest it is among the largest dwarf planet candidates ever found beyond Neptune.
Astronomers spotted the provisionally named object in data from the Simonyi Survey Telescope at the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. It had likely escaped earlier searches because millions of Milky Way stars crowded the view, making even a world this large difficult to pick out.
A possible sixth dwarf planet
Its distance, brightness, and estimated surface reflectivity suggest a diameter of 600 to 1,500 kilometers, or about 370 to 930 miles. Icy bodies that large are expected to have enough gravity to pull themselves into a round shape, one requirement for dwarf planet status. More observations are needed to measure ED138’s exact size and confirm whether it qualifies.
2026 ED138 orbital arc (with annotations). Credit: NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA
If confirmed, ED138 would join the five dwarf planets recognized by the International Astronomical Union: Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea, and Makemake.
Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, first identified the candidate. He and Mario Jurić, a University of Washington professor of astronomy and leader of Rubin’s solar system team, presented the results at a press conference on October 27, 2026. Jurić contributed additional observations that helped establish the object’s orbit.
“Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation,” Jurić said. “It’s the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope.”
Mosaic of 2026 ED138 discovery images. Credit: NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA
ED138 is currently about 46 astronomical units (au) from the Sun. One au is the average distance between Earth and the Sun, and Pluto’s average distance is about 40 au. ED138 belongs to a population called trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs), which orbit the Sun beyond Neptune.
The sizes, compositions, and orbits of these distant objects offer clues to how the solar system formed. Scientists study them to understand how the giant planets migrated over time and how smaller bodies were scattered as the system evolved.
Spotting motion among millions of stars
Finding ED138 required distinguishing its movement from the crowded stellar background near the plane of the Milky Way. Rubin repeatedly monitors the entire southern sky, while powerful algorithms sift through millions to billions of points of light to identify small moving objects. Together, those capabilities allowed the team to pick ED138 out of a field where it had been difficult for other telescopes to detect.
On the evening of October 13, Holman was processing Rubin observations collected earlier in 2026 with search code he had developed with colleague Kevin Napier. The code compares billions of detections of moving objects and determines which detections belong to the same body. When ED138 appeared in the results, its brightness and distance immediately suggested that it was unusually large.
“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said. “Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.”
This image from the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory shows the area of sky where the newly discovered dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138 (ED138) was found. This image is a composite of multiple images captured by Rubin between 4 March and 11 July 2026. Credit: NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA
Jurić searched Rubin’s catalogs and images and located 20 more observations stretching back to March 2026. The team also found ED138 in archival images from other surveys dating to 2016. Those records allowed the researchers to trace more than 10 years of its orbit.
“Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision,” Jurić said. “And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and ‘precover’ objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system.”
Top-down view of 2026 ED138 orbit (with dwarf planets). Credit: NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/R. Proctor Image Processing: M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Orbit data provided by the IAU Minor Planet Center (MPCorb catalog), funded by NASA PDCO and the Tamkin Foundation. Star map: NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center Scientific Visualization Studio. Gaia DR2: ESA/Gaia/DPAC
A ten-year search for overlooked worlds
ED138 adds to a rapidly growing collection of solar system objects discovered by Rubin since it began gathering early data in preparation for the
Legacy Survey of Space and Time
, or LSST. The survey began in June 2026. In April, before its formal start, Rubin’s solar system team announced observations of more than
11,000 new asteroids
, with roughly 380 new TNOs included in the announcement. The team called that submission “the tip of the iceberg” and expressed excitement about the discoveries to come once LSST began.
“If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds,” Holman said. “Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for 10 years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach.”
Operations of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory are funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Science.

title: New Research Identifies the Hidden Rules That Help Brain Cancer Evade Treatment
content:
Glioblastoma is the most common and aggressive malignant brain tumor in adults. It grows rapidly, infiltrates surrounding brain tissue, and is extremely difficult to treat. Credit: Shutterstock
Scientists have discovered hidden rules governing how glioblastoma cells change states and resist treatment.
Glioblastoma is one of the deadliest brain cancers, partly because its cells can change identities to survive treatment. Now, two studies published in
reveal that these changes follow predictable patterns, potentially offering new ways to make the tumors less aggressive.
Researchers from EMBL, the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ), and the Wellcome Sanger Institute discovered that glioblastoma cells transition between distinct states according to specific molecular rules. Some cells resemble neurons, others share features with stem cells, and some adopt aggressive, injury-like states. This flexibility, known as cellular plasticity, helps tumors resist therapy.
Mapping the Hidden Patterns of Brain Cancer
To investigate these changes, scientists analyzed DNA, RNA, and epigenetic information from tumors collected from 12 patients, creating one of the most comprehensive molecular atlases of glioblastoma.
“We asked – can we go back to the drawing board?” said Omer Bayraktar of the Wellcome Sanger Institute. “Can we assume that we know nothing about this disease, and reconstruct how a cancer cell behaves in glioblastoma through quantitative approaches?”
“We wanted to figure out whether there is a specific rule-based system that determines how cells transition between these states,” said Oliver Stegle of EMBL Heidelberg and DKFZ. “And we asked not only whether there were rules, but also what would drive such rules.”
The analysis showed that cancer cells follow recurring paths between states rather than switching randomly. Different cell states also occupy specific regions within tumors, a pattern researchers confirmed using laboratory-grown tumor organoids.
“By integrating the single-cell data with spatial transcriptomic data, we found that there is a meticulous and very specific spatial architecture of cancer cell states,” explained Bayraktar. “And this was present in every single glioblastoma tumor in every single patient we studied.”
AI Uncovers the Molecular Controls
Researchers then examined gene regulation in more than one million patient-derived glioblastoma cells. Using a deep learning tool called scDORI, they identified molecular regulators that influence how cancer cells change states. Some act as safeguards, keeping cells in relatively stable states and limiting their plasticity.
“A tumor generates an almost endless number of variations on its own regulatory program,” said Stegle. “Instead of seeing this heterogeneity only as an obstacle, we can use AI to learn from it and extract the rules that determine how cells choose their fate.”
The findings suggested that manipulating a small number of regulators might redirect cancer cells toward less aggressive states.
“One of our premises has always been that when we understand these rules, we can not only observe what the cells are doing, but we can also change what they are doing,” said Moritz Mall of DKFZ. “We could perhaps reprogram them, and maybe push them into a state that is less malignant, less dangerous.”
Reprogramming Tumor Cells Shows Promise
Experiments supported this possibility. Increasing the activity of MYT1L, one of the identified regulators, reduced cellular plasticity and malignant characteristics in patient-derived glioblastoma cells. Mice transplanted with these modified tumor cells survived longer than those receiving control cells.
“The results with MYT1L were interesting, but the findings go much beyond that,” explained Mall. “Our approach predicts the regulators for all of the major tumor cell states, and we tested those predictions experimentally. We were able to steer tumor cells into specific states by manipulating just a handful of regulators.”
Although clinical treatments remain a future possibility, researchers are already applying the approach to other cancers and brain disorders.
“With the help of this atlas and the new AI tool, we identified new regulatory sequences that enable us to potentially drive specific cell states in a tumor-specific setting,” said Mall. “Now that we have this framework, we can apply it to many other questions and cancers.”
