title: New Study Challenges Long-Held Fears About Exercise and Knee Damage
content:
Knee osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint condition in which cartilage, the smooth tissue that cushions the ends of bones, gradually breaks down. Credit: Shutterstock
Recovering from ACL reconstruction doesn’t always mean the end of knee problems, with many young adults facing persistent pain and an increased risk of early-onset osteoarthritis.
ACL reconstruction does not always restore long-term knee health. About half of patients remain dissatisfied with their knees two years after surgery, and roughly half develop early-onset osteoarthritis within a decade. New research from La Trobe University suggests that targeted exercise and education can help young adults manage persistent knee problems without worsening cartilage damage.
The findings come from the SUPER-Knee clinical trial, which involved 184 adults ages 18 to 40 who continued experiencing knee problems one to three years after ACL reconstruction. Researchers compared a four-month progressive exercise program supervised by physiotherapists with a single education session. Participants following the exercise program experienced improvements in pain, quality of life, and muscle strength, with no detected deterioration in knee cartilage or early osteoarthritis.
Challenging Long-Held Concerns About Exercise and Knee Damage
Although clinical guidelines recommend exercise-based rehabilitation and education after ACL surgery, many patients do not receive care that follows these recommendations. Concerns that exercise could damage knee cartilage also persist among patients and healthcare professionals.
The SUPER-Knee trial, published in the
Annals of Internal Medicine
, was the first to investigate this approach more than nine months after ACL reconstruction, a point when patients are generally expected to have recovered but often still experience difficulties.
“Currently we don’t have any high-quality evidence for what treatments should be offered to young people at risk of early-onset knee osteoarthritis. Our SUPER-Knee study changes this, and addresses a globally recognized research priority,” said lead researcher Associate Professor Adam Culvenor.
“Our study showed physiotherapist-supervised exercise therapy and education is safe and should be recommended to improve the knee health of young people at high risk of early-onset osteoarthritis following ACL reconstruction.”
Years of Pain After ACL Reconstruction
For Ruby Cumming, the challenges of recovery extended far beyond the sports field. She tore her ACL while playing Australian rules football in 2019, when she was 24, and underwent reconstructive surgery within six weeks. Despite regularly attending physiotherapy and performing rehabilitation exercises, she experienced daily pain for three to four years and never returned to football.
“I thought if I had the surgery and did the rehab I’d be able to get back to normal. After surgery impacted my entire life – not just footy – I changed my outlook and decided I wanted to avoid re-injuring my knee ever again so haven’t played contact sport since,” Ruby said.
“Experiencing regular pain, not being able to walk, getting public transport to work and living independently all became really challenging for me.”
Her symptoms improved after she enrolled in the SUPER-Knee program and began attending weekly supervised rehabilitation sessions. “When I joined the SUPER-Knee program and did weekly physio-supervised rehab, this improved my pain significantly,” Ruby said.
A Potential Shift in ACL Rehabilitation Guidelines
The researchers believe the findings could influence how clinicians treat younger patients who continue to experience knee problems long after reconstruction, particularly those at elevated risk of developing osteoarthritis.
“The evidence generated by the SUPER-Knee trial can be used to update international clinical practice guidelines for rehabilitation following ACL reconstruction and could be a lifeline for young people struggling after serious knee injuries.”
The program is also designed to be practical for routine clinical care rather than requiring specialized rehabilitation facilities. “The intervention is ready to be used by local health professionals with minimal specialized equipment or staff training.”
Although the trial demonstrated improvements in knee health without detected cartilage deterioration during the study, whether the intervention prevents osteoarthritis over the longer term remains to be established.

title: Smiling Isn’t Always Good for You, Scientists Discover
content:
Smiling is a universal form of human expression that communicates emotions, strengthens social connections, and can influence how we feel. Credit: Shutterstock
A new study reveals that smiling can sometimes backfire, challenging long-held assumptions about facial expressions and happiness.
Smiling might make you feel happier, but doing it repeatedly under pressure can have the opposite effect. New psychological research suggests that the emotional benefits of smiling depend on how often people do it, whether they feel compelled to, and the circumstances surrounding the expression.
In an experiment involving more than 1,100 participants, researchers found that a single posed smile could provide a modest boost in happiness. However, repeating the expression or facing financial consequences for failing to smile sometimes reduced happiness instead. The findings challenge the assumption that deliberately smiling is always beneficial.
Why a Psychology Researcher Began Questioning Smiling
Nicholas Coles, Ph.D., a professor of psychology at the University of Florida, had spent years investigating whether facial expressions influence emotions. Although his earlier research supported the idea that smiling can improve mood, his experiences working in customer service seemed to contradict those findings.
“I used to work in customer service. I actually got written up for my inability to keep smiling at work at an unnamed theme park in Florida,” laughed Coles. “So I’m looking at all this evidence I had accrued so far that smiling boosts happiness and realizing it flies in the face of my own experiences in the world.”
To investigate that contradiction, Coles collaborated with Annabel Dang and Joao Francisco Goes Braga Takayanagi on an experiment designed to introduce workplace pressures into traditional studies of smiling. Their findings were published October 1 in the
Journal of Experimental Social Psychology
Putting Forced Smiles to the Test
The researchers recruited 1,201 people for an online experiment, ultimately including 1,174 in their analysis. Participants viewed pleasant images, such as kittens and flowers, or disturbing images depicting theft and animal mistreatment. Some were instructed to smile, while others were allowed to respond with their natural facial expressions. Depending on their assigned condition, they completed the exercise either once or 10 times.
To simulate workplace pressure, half the participants were warned that failing to follow the smiling instructions could cost them $2 of their $6 payment. Everyone ultimately received the full amount, regardless of their performance. Participants rated their happiness after each task, allowing the researchers to compare how repetition and financial pressure affected their emotional responses.
“We tried to combine the classic way of studying it in a lab with some extra ingredients that we might see in the real world. We told participants that we would pay them less if they weren’t successfully smiling,” Coles said. “We also controlled the number of times they have to do it, because in customer service, every interaction is another faked smile.”
When Smiling Stops Improving Happiness
For participants viewing unpleasant images, posing a single smile produced a small improvement in happiness compared with responding naturally. The benefit appeared even among those warned about losing money. However, repeating the smile weakened the positive effect, and combining repetition with financial pressure eliminated it.
The pattern differed when participants viewed pleasant images. A single posed smile produced little change in happiness, but repeated smiling or the threat of financial penalties made participants less happy than those who responded naturally. Additional analysis indicated that forced smiling under these pleasant conditions also tended to increase irritation and anger.
“If you only force a smile once without any financial penalties, you can see the improvement in happiness. So what psychologists were seeing in their lab is right,” he said. “But when you make it a little bit more like the real world, where you have to keep repeating it, and if you don’t do it well, you get financial penalties, you see it completely reverse.”
What the Findings Mean for Workplace Smiling
The results suggest that research demonstrating the benefits of smiling does not necessarily apply to situations where people must maintain cheerful expressions throughout the day. Repetition and external pressure can change the emotional effects of an otherwise positive facial expression.
The findings also have implications for customer service policies. Target, for example, faced criticism over a policy requiring employees to smile when customers came within a specified distance. Coles argues that such expectations can restrict workers’ freedom to express their genuine emotions while also placing pressure on customers to reciprocate expressions of friendliness.
After years of researching ways to increase happiness, Coles has also begun questioning society’s emphasis on constantly improving emotional well-being rather than accepting existing feelings.
“As a society, we have placed such an immense amount of emphasis on trying to make ourselves feel happier than we currently are,” he said, “much less emphasis on just being content with what we have.”
Reference: “Smiling your way to happiness or misery? Experimental tests of competing perspectives [Registered Report – stage II]” by Nicholas A. Coles, Annabel V. Dang and Joao Francisco Goes Braga Takayanagi, 1 October 2026,
Journal of Experimental Social Psychology

title: Scientists Discover Greenland’s Ice Sheet Once Retreated 60 Miles
content:
Tundra vegetation is seen on the Greenland landscape in this photo from 2012. A University at Buffalo-led study found that summer temperatures at Camp Century on Greenland were 4.7 degrees Celsisus higher during an ice-free period 416,000 years ago. Credit: Josh Brown, University of Vermont
Sediment beneath a secret Cold War base reveals a time when warmer summers helped push Greenland’s ice more than 60 miles back from its current edge.
About 416,000 years ago, the ground beneath Greenland’s Camp Century was exposed to the sky. A new University at Buffalo-led study estimates that summers there were 4.7 degrees Celsius (8.5 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than today, offering a rare glimpse of the conditions that accompanied a major retreat of the ice sheet.
“It’s striking that a period of moderately warmer temperatures coincided with such a substantial retreat of the ice sheet,” says lead author John Michael Aguilar, a postdoctoral fellow at the UB RENEW Institute.
A Climate Record Beneath A Cold War Base
Camp Century housed the U.S. Army’s
failed Project Iceworm
, a secret plan to hide nuclear missiles beneath Greenland’s ice. During drilling in the 1960s, researchers recovered sediment from nearly a mile (1.6 kilometers) below the surface. Those samples have since become an unlikely archive of Greenland’s climate.
Earlier work showed that
the sediment last saw sunlight approximately 416,000 years ago
. Exposing the ground at Camp Century would have required the ice sheet’s edge in that region to retreat more than 60 miles (97 kilometers) from its present position.
The new study goes beyond establishing that the ice disappeared. By examining fatty molecules produced by bacteria and preserved in the sediment, the team reconstructed the summer temperatures that accompanied that retreat.
“The types and proportions of these molecules change depending on the temperature,” Aguilar says. “By comparing them with similar molecules found in modern Arctic lakes, we were able to estimate how warm it was at Camp Century.”
The study’s findings come from ancient sediment recovered from nearly a mile below the ice sheet at Camp Century in the 1960’s. Credit: Andrew Christ, University of Vermont
Why the Length of Warming Matters
The researchers believe their findings provide the first quantitative estimate of summer temperatures on land anywhere in Greenland during this ancient warm period. Such records are exceptionally difficult to recover because later advances of the ice sheet eroded most sediment from that time.
Surprisingly, Camp Century remained covered by ice even when Greenland experienced similarly warm summers roughly 5,000 to 10,000 years ago, after the last Ice Age.
One possible explanation is that the earlier warm period lasted much longer, potentially tens of thousands of years. Sustained warmth would have given the ice sheet more time to melt, suggesting that peak temperatures alone cannot explain how far it retreats.
“This work gives us a better understanding of how the ice sheet responds to sustained warming and what may be possible in the future,” says corresponding author Elizabeth Thomas, PhD, an associate professor in the Department of Earth Sciences in UB’s College of Arts and Sciences.
What Ancient Melting Means for Greenland’s Future
The findings arrive as scientists anticipate substantial Arctic warming. Depending on emissions, average annual Arctic temperatures could rise by 3.3 to 10 degrees Celsius (5.9 to 18 degrees Fahrenheit) by the end of this century, according to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).
With that warming ahead, Thomas cautions against assuming that Greenland’s ice will respond as slowly as it did during the ancient warm period.
“Today’s human-caused warming is more intense than the warm period 400,000 years ago,” Thomas says. “And climate projections suggest that this warmth could persist for hundreds or thousands of years. Both the magnitude and duration of warming are important to understanding how the ice sheet will respond.”
Forgotten Sediment, Decades of Discovery
The samples nearly slipped out of scientific view. Chester Langway, who led the Camp Century ice core drilling, brought them to UB in 1975. They remained in its Central Ice Core Storage Facility and Information Exchange until his retirement in the mid-1990s, then spent more than two decades largely forgotten at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark.
A chance freezer cleanout in 2018 brought the sediment back to researchers’ attention. Thomas has studied it with University of Vermont collaborators ever since, and its remarkable history became the subject of an
Emmy Award-winning documentary
For Thomas, the latest study brings years of work with Aguilar together. Measuring the molecules was familiar territory; translating them into a reliable comparison with modern temperatures was much harder.
“The type of molecular analysis we did in this study is something we do all the time in my lab, but interpreting the results was unusually challenging. We had to account for how the land’s elevation changed as the ice sheet grew and melted, which affects how temperatures can be compared across time,” Thomas says. “What may look like a routine analysis actually took years to figure out. It’s been quite a journey, not unlike the journey these sediment samples took to get here.”

title: Researchers Recover DNA from 7,000-Year-Old Leather, Revealing a Link to Goats Alive Today
content:
Approximately 7,000-year-old tanned goat leather preserved in Cueva de los Murciélagos, Albuñol (Granada, Spain), from which ancient DNA was recovered for this study. Credit: MUTERMUR Project,
CC-BY 4.0
Ancient DNA recovered from a remarkably preserved piece of 7,000-year-old leather is shedding new light on how prehistoric communities in Spain used domesticated animals.
A 7,000-year-old piece of goat leather discovered in a Spanish burial cave has yielded ancient DNA, allowing scientists to trace a genetic connection between prehistoric livestock and goats living in Spain today. The exceptionally preserved material also provides direct evidence that Early Neolithic communities were processing the hides of domesticated animals.
The findings, published November 4, 2026, in the journal
PLOS One
, come from a study led by Jolijn A. M. Erven of University College Dublin and colleagues. Their analysis offers a rare glimpse into animal husbandry and leatherworking on the Iberian Peninsula thousands of years before written records.
Ancient Leather Preserves Evidence of Prehistoric Craftsmanship
The leather fragment was recovered from Cueva de los Murciélagos, a burial site in southern Spain known for preserving ancient organic materials. Radiocarbon dating placed the specimen at approximately 7,000 years old. Marks on its surface indicate that the hide had been tanned and perforated, suggesting it was once part of a garment or protective covering before being buried alongside human remains.
Recovering DNA from such ancient leather is particularly difficult in warmer regions, where heat and environmental conditions accelerate the breakdown of genetic material. Despite extensive fragmentation, researchers extracted both mitochondrial DNA, which is inherited through the maternal line, and nuclear DNA, which contains genetic information from both parents.
A Bermeya goat from the Principality of Asturias, Spain, one of the modern breeds showing the closest genetic affinity to the Neolithic goat from Cueva de los Murciélagos. Credit: MUTERMUR Project in collaboration with ACRIBER,
CC-BY 4.0
Francisco Martínez-Sevilla emphasized the unusual preservation conditions: “The preservation of this 7,000-year-old goat leather is exceptional. Cueva de los Murciélagos has preserved organic materials that rarely survive in the archaeological record, offering us a unique opportunity to investigate prehistoric technologies, animal husbandry, and the relationships between human communities and domestic animals.”
Ancient DNA Connects Neolithic Goats With Modern Spanish Breeds
Genetic analysis identified the leather as coming from a domestic goat rather than a wild Iberian ibex. Its DNA showed a close relationship to the modern Bermeya goat breed of northern Spain, indicating that a related genetic lineage has persisted on the Iberian Peninsula for thousands of years.
The researchers also detected no evidence of African genetic ancestry in the ancient specimen, unlike the ancestry found in modern European goats. One possible explanation is that genetic exchange involving African goat populations occurred after the Neolithic period. However, the incomplete DNA and limited sample size prevent firm conclusions about when these connections developed or what they might indicate about prehistoric interactions between Iberia and Africa.
Kevin Daly highlighted the genetic link between ancient and living animals: “It is rare to for such ancient, organic materials to retain DNA – but this was one of the few exceptions. With a tiny amount of surviving DNA, we were able to show a link with Iberian breeds today – a genetic connection spanning 7,000 years. This study demonstrates what can done through the collaboration of international multidisciplinary teams – transforming an archaeological object into a link with the living present.”

title: Scientists Discover Climate Change May Have Stopped Earth’s Next Ice Age
content:
Scientists have uncovered evidence that Earth may have been entering a new glacial period thousands of years ago before rising temperatures abruptly reversed the process. Credit: SciTechDaily.com
A new glacial period may have been taking shape in the Arctic until global warming brought its slow advance to a halt.
An ice cap in northern Canada began expanding about 2,000 years ago, according to research published in
. The researchers argue that this growth marked the beginning of Earth’s next glacial period. By the 1960s, however, warmer summers had reversed the process, causing the ice to retreat.
“It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen—and yet it stopped,” says Nicolás Young, a geochemist at the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, part of the Columbia Climate School. “It’s a very powerful example of how we have jolted the system.”
Young, fellow Lamont geochemist Joerg Schaefer, and their colleagues investigated the surviving remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet. That enormous ice mass covered much of Canada and the northern United States from about 95,000 to 20,000 years ago. At its largest, it extended from above the Arctic Circle to Illinois, with ice more than two miles (3.2 kilometers) thick in places.
The Ice Sheet That Never Fully Disappeared
Today, the Laurentide survives as the Barnes Ice Cap, an ice mass roughly the size of Delaware on central Baffin Island in Nunavut, Canada. “People always say that it disappeared, but that’s not true,” says Young.
The Laurentide repeatedly expanded and retreated after widespread continental glaciation began about 2.6 million years ago. The team wanted to determine whether its remaining ice had once occupied an even smaller area than it does today before growing again.
The end of a glaciation. Prominent trimline marks the 1960 extent of the Barnes Ice Cap. The dark-colored landscape hosts mature vegetation and lichen cover, whereas the light-colored rock is vegetation-free. Ice margin retreat from this trimline has reversed ~2,000 years of ice margin expansion. Credit: Nicolás Young
Finding the moment an ice sheet stopped shrinking and began rebuilding is difficult because advancing glaciers usually erase the evidence of their earlier boundaries. Barnes offered an unusual way around that problem: plants preserved beneath the ice.
Buried Plants Reveal The Ice’s Return
Unlike most glaciers, the Barnes Ice Cap is frozen to its bedrock and does not slide over the ground. When it expanded, it buried vegetation instead of scraping it away. Its retreat since 1960 has gradually exposed those preserved plants.
Researchers dated the vegetation using carbon-14, a harmlessly radioactive form of atmospheric carbon that living organisms absorb. After an organism dies, its carbon-14 decays at a predictable rate, allowing scientists to estimate when the plants died as the ice advanced over them.
Margin of the Barnes Ice Cap. Bedrock has only become exposed sometime over the last decade. Credit: Nicolás Young.
“If you do this enough times, you can actually develop a timeline of that ice margin systematically advancing over plants. You’re actually tracking the expansion of that ice margin,” says Young.
Combining samples from Barnes with vegetation exposed by recently melted smaller ice caps nearby, the team reconstructed the region’s climate history. The Laurentide reached its smallest extent about 3,000 years ago. Roughly 1,000 years later, conditions became cold enough for ice to accumulate again.
When Does A Glacial Period Begin?
The researchers propose that this first renewed growth should count as the beginning of a glacial period. That definition places the starting point long before ice sheets spread across continents.
Earlier modeling studies have suggested that the next glaciation would remain thousands or even tens of thousands of years away. Young and his colleagues argue that waiting for enormous continental ice sheets to form overlooks the much earlier stages of their development.
Their findings also revisit controversial claims made by some climate scientists in the 1970s that another ice age was approaching. “It actually was happening,” Young says. “They couldn’t quite prove it, but now we sort of have the evidence.”
The process would have unfolded far too slowly to transform the climate within a human lifetime. Young says noticeable cooling would have taken thousands of years, while restoring Laurentide’s continental reach would have required about 30,000 years. In the team’s interpretation, warming interrupted that process near its beginning.
A Vanishing Starting Point for Future Ice Sheets
Its loss could also reshape the conditions for future glaciations. The Laurentide once provided a ready starting point for expansion when the climate cooled. Its frigid mass supported feedback processes that encouraged more ice to accumulate.
With greenhouse gas concentrations elevated, scientists cannot say when another glaciation might begin. If continental ice sheets eventually grow again, they may have to develop without this surviving foundation.
“What has been an extremely natural and predictable phenomenon is now gone,” says Young.

title: Strange Materials Make Waves Behave in Ways That Defy Expectations
content:
Artistic rendering of a hyperbolic wave attractor forming in an odd-shaped cavity inside a hyperbolic material. Credit: Andrea Alu
Researchers have uncovered an unusual wave phenomenon that links engineered materials to principles found in ocean physics.
Waves bouncing around an irregularly shaped space typically follow increasingly unpredictable paths. Scientists have now shown that certain materials can produce the opposite effect, guiding waves into stable, repeating patterns instead of chaotic trajectories.
Researchers at the Advanced Science Research Center at the CUNY Graduate Center (CUNY ASRC) discovered this behavior in hyperbolic materials, whose unusual properties restrict the directions in which waves can travel. Their study, published in
Nature Physics
, identifies structures called “hyperbolic wave attractors” that could eventually help engineers control light, sound, and electromagnetic signals.
“This work shows how geometry and the properties of a material can work together to produce wave behavior that is both surprising and useful,” said Andrea Alù, the study’s principal investigator, director of the Photonics Initiative at the CUNY ASRC, and Distinguished Professor of Physics at the CUNY Graduate Center. “By understanding how waves organize themselves in these hyperbolic media, we can begin to explore new approaches to controlling energy, information, and communication signals in complex environments.”
When Waves Defy the Usual Rules of Reflection
In ordinary materials, waves generally reflect at the same angle at which they strike a surface. Repeated reflections inside an irregular enclosure can produce chaotic motion, a phenomenon studied through a classic physics problem known as a dynamical billiard.
Hyperbolic materials behave differently. Named after the mathematical curve called a hyperbola, these materials direct waves along specific paths and alter how they reflect from angled surfaces. Inside an irregular cavity, these unusual reflection rules can cause waves to converge toward organized trajectories.
“Normally, we expect a complicated cavity to produce complicated, chaotic wave patterns,” said Simon Yves, a postdoctoral researcher in Alù’s lab and a first author of the study. “Here, the opposite happens. The unusual propagation and reflection of waves create a strong geometric organization, producing well-defined paths that can persist across a broad range of wavelengths.”
How Waves Organize Into Stable Patterns
The researchers found that repeated reflections can guide waves into closed trajectories that remain stable across different scales. This behavior arises partly from broken mirror symmetry in the reflection process, which causes wavelengths to progressively shrink as waves travel through the cavity.
These wave attractors also exhibit handedness, meaning their paths circulate clockwise or counterclockwise. Their stability and direction depend on the geometry of the cavity and the material’s unusual wave properties. The team demonstrated the phenomenon using a mechanical metamaterial engineered to control vibrations.
“The most exciting aspect of these results is that they connect a simple geometric idea with a rich set of wave phenomena,” said Enrico Renzi, a doctoral student in Alù’s lab and a first author of the study. “We can observe how the waves become organized, and we can connect that organization to properties such as stability and handedness. This gives us a framework for designing wave behavior rather than simply observing it.”
Related wave attractors occur in oceans, where internal waves traveling through water layers of different densities reflect unusually from underwater slopes. These reflections can concentrate energy along closed paths and contribute to wave turbulence.
The new study demonstrates a similar effect in an engineered solid, allowing researchers to investigate the underlying physics in a controlled laboratory setting. The principles could also extend to hyperbolic phonon polaritons, hybrid light and matter excitations found in certain crystals, including hexagonal boron nitride and molybdenum trioxide.
These materials can confine infrared light to extremely small regions, making them promising candidates for nanophotonic technologies. Potential applications of hyperbolic wave attractors include compact optical circuits, optical signal separation, particle trapping, analog wave computing, and sensitive biological sensors, although these uses have not yet been demonstrated.
“This research opens a path toward engineering stable and robust wave patterns in systems where waves would normally be expected to rapidly become chaotic,” Alù said. “Our goal is to understand how these effects can be harnessed to create new functionalities for photonics, phononics, and wave-based technologies.”
Reference: “Hyperbolic wave attractors” by Simon Yves, Enrico M. Renzi, Sander A. Mann and Andrea Alù, 28 September 2026,
Nature Physics
DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03453-7
The research was supported by the Simons Foundation and the National Science Foundation Science and Technology Center “New Frontiers of Sound.

title: Quantum Discovery Reveals Why More Powerful Lasers Can Actually Slow Atoms Down
content:
Two synchronized light pulses induce an amplified sliding vibration in the atomic layers of WTe
. Credit: Gerrit Horstmann
Researchers have uncovered an unexpected way to control the movement of atomic layers in quantum materials.
Scientists have discovered that two carefully timed laser pulses can move atomic layers in a quantum material more effectively than a single, more powerful pulse. Published in
Nature Physics
, the research shows that increasing light intensity can actually limit atomic motion, while controlling when the energy arrives can overcome that restriction.
The discovery comes from researchers at the Universities of Würzburg and Rostock and ETH Zurich, who investigated tungsten ditelluride (WTe
), a material known as a sliding ferroelectric. Its neighboring atomic layers can shift sideways against each other, much like two palms pressed together.
“What makes this particularly exciting is that the relative motion of the atomic layers can influence a range of material properties, such as ferroelectricity and topology,” explains Gerrit Horstmann, first author of the study and head of an Emmy Noether junior research group at the University of Würzburg.
Why Stronger Laser Pulses Can Slow Atomic Motion
Ultrashort laser pulses can change a crystal’s structure by transferring energy to its electrons. As the electrons respond, they exert forces on atomic nuclei, setting the atoms in motion. These processes occur within femtoseconds, with each femtosecond lasting just one millionth of a billionth of a second.
Increasing the laser’s intensity might seem like an obvious way to produce greater movement, but the researchers found that this approach has a fundamental limitation. “Under very strong excitation, electrons are promoted into high-energy states that counteract the directed motion of the atoms. The additional light energy then no longer produces a correspondingly larger displacement of the atomic layers; instead, it effectively slows them down,” explains Gerrit Horstmann.
Using Two Laser Pulses to Control Quantum Materials
To bypass this limitation, the team divided the laser energy between two weaker pulses delivered at different times. After the first pulse, the excited electrons have time to partially relax before the second pulse arrives. By adjusting the delay, the researchers can reinforce the sliding motion of the atomic layers, similar to pushing a child on a swing at precisely the right moment.
“Timing opens up an additional way to make optimal use of the interaction between electrons and atomic motion,” says Horstmann. Rather than forcing the atoms to move with increasingly powerful pulses, the technique uses the material’s own electronic and atomic dynamics to achieve more effective control. The approach follows a familiar principle: “Work smarter, not harder!”
A Possible Path to More Energy-Efficient Electronics
Controlling how atomic layers slide could eventually provide a way to switch technologically useful properties, including ferroelectric polarization, with less energy. The technique may be particularly valuable for ultrathin materials such as WTe
, which can consist of only a few atomic layers and are being explored for compact electronic devices.
Although practical applications remain a longer-term goal, the findings establish a strategy for manipulating quantum materials through the timing of light pulses rather than simply increasing their intensity. As the researchers put it, “Work smarter, not harder!”
Reference: “Coherent phonon control beyond amplitude saturation in a sliding ferroelectric” by Jan Gerrit Horstmann, Christoph Emeis, Andrin Caviezel, Quintin N. Meier, Nicolas Wyler, Thomas Lottermoser, Fabio Caruso and Manfred Fiebig, 21 October 2026,
Nature Physics
DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03491-1

title: Einstein Was Right Again: Scientists Discover Chemical Bonds That Defy Textbook Rules
content:
Chemistry
Chemical bonds hold atoms together through interactions involving electrons. New research shows that Einstein’s theory of relativity can alter triple bonds in heavy elements, challenging traditional explanations of how atoms connect. Credit: Shutterstock
Scientists have uncovered direct evidence that Einstein’s theory of relativity changes how atoms form triple chemical bonds in heavy elements.
A fundamental rule of chemical bonding begins to break down when atoms become sufficiently heavy. Chemists at
Brown University
have found direct experimental evidence that Einstein’s theory of relativity changes the structure of triple bonds, challenging a model that has been taught in chemistry classrooms for generations.
The discovery, published in
, comes from experiments involving carbon and bismuth, a heavy element whose electrons are strongly influenced by relativistic effects. “This idea that relativity is important in heavy elements has been around since the 1970s,” said Lai-Sheng Wang, a Brown chemistry professor and the study’s corresponding author. “But we show direct spectroscopic evidence that what we learned in high school about chemical bonding isn’t true in heavy elements.”
How Relativity Changes Chemical Bonds
Chemical bonds form when atoms share electrons, creating an attraction that holds their positively charged nuclei together. In the conventional description of a triple bond, three shared electron pairs produce one sigma bond and two pi bonds. The sigma bond forms through direct overlap along the axis connecting the nuclei, while the pi bonds involve electron density extending to either side of that axis.
This arrangement accurately describes many bonds involving lighter elements. In heavier atoms, however, the strong positive charge of the nucleus causes some electrons to move at speeds where relativistic effects become significant. These effects strengthen a phenomenon called spin-orbit coupling, which links an electron’s spin to its orbital motion and changes how electrons participate in bonding.
“The boundary between a sigma bond and a pi bond is now sort of smeared,” Wang said. “We still have three bonds, but we don’t really strictly have a sigma or a pi anymore.”
Experiments Reveal a Different Triple Bond
To investigate this effect, Brown doctoral students Deniz Kahraman and Jie Hui, working with Wang and their colleagues, produced molecules containing carbon and bismuth. They cooled the molecules to temperatures near absolute zero before examining them with photoelectron spectroscopy, a technique that uses light to eject electrons and measures their energies to determine how strongly they were bound.
The resulting spectra provided evidence of a triple bond unlike the conventional arrangement. Instead of one sigma bond and two pi bonds, the carbon-bismuth bond exhibited characteristics consistent with one pi bond and two hybrid sigma-pi bonds. This experimentally observed structure supports theoretical predictions that relativistic spin-orbit coupling can fundamentally alter bonding in heavy elements.
Implications for Future Materials
The findings could influence how chemists describe bonds involving heavy elements, particularly as researchers explore their potential in advanced technologies. Bismuth has attracted attention as a possible alternative to toxic lead in next-generation solar cells. It is also being investigated in quantum materials and research relevant to quantum computing.
Understanding how relativistic effects influence its chemical bonds may help scientists develop more accurate descriptions of bismuth-containing compounds and other heavy-element materials. The new evidence could eventually change how these bonds are presented in chemistry textbooks.
“Maybe this will become the new textbook idea as we are dealing with more and more heavy chemistry of the heavy elements,” Wang said.
Reference: “Relativistic collapse of the classical triple bond in the CBi− molecular ion” by Deniz Kahraman, Jie Hui, Xin-Yu Zhang, Neil A. Ellis, Hyun Wook Choi, Kirk A. Peterson and Lai-Sheng Wang, 9 July 2026,
DOI: 10.1126/science.aei1285
The work was funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation (CHE-2403841) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-SC0008501).

title: Scientists Discover a Hidden Eye Disease That Can Steal Your Night Vision
content:
Scientists have identified a rare genetic eye disease that can develop silently for decades before causing progressive vision loss. Credit: Shutterstock
Researchers can spot signs of a newly identified genetic eye disease before light-sensing cells are lost by measuring how vision recovers in darkness.
People with a newly identified genetic eye condition can see well for most of their lives before gradually losing peripheral vision and struggling to see at dusk or at night. The condition is linked to a gene already associated with a different eye disease, one that affects central vision first.
The two conditions arise from different variants, or versions, of the
gene. The newly identified variant, p.Arg140Trp, causes abnormally thick material to build up between cells in the eye. Researchers are calling the condition
-associated late-onset retinal degeneration, or L-ORD, although it has not been formally named.
Slow adjustment to darkness offers a clue
L-ORD begins slowly at the periphery of the retina, the tissue at the back of the eye that converts light into signals the brain interprets as sight. Its gradual progression makes it difficult to detect. One useful clue is unusually slow recovery of vision when a person moves from a lighted setting into low light. This adjustment involves rod photoreceptors, the retinal cells specialized for seeing in dim conditions.
“We can detect a major abnormality in the way rod photoreceptors recover in darkness with retinas that still look structurally intact,” said Artur V. Cideciyan, PhD, an ophthalmology researcher and co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. “This gives us a functional marker of disease at a stage when photoreceptor cells have not yet been lost.”
One gene, two patterns of vision loss
The investigation began with a clinical description of a family in the United States in 1998.
“The different disease expression in this family was thought to be similar to a condition caused by
gene variants. However, none of the variants associated with that disease were found,” Cideciyan said. “Our collaborators then discovered a new variant in the
gene that normally causes a different disease where the macula, which is tied to central vision, is affected first.”
The genetic finding allowed researchers to expand the investigation to multiple European families. They studied three unrelated families in different countries that shared the p.Arg140Trp variant and compared them with a separate family carrying p.Arg345Trp, the
variant responsible for the already-known condition affecting central vision.
Possible clues to common retinal diseases
The researchers do not yet know how widespread p.Arg140Trp is or how many people have this form of L-ORD. They suspect it may be relatively rare, but larger studies are needed to establish its prevalence.
“Aging is a risk factor for many medical conditions, including retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration, the most common retinal condition of aging,” said Tomas S. Aleman, MD, a professor of ophthalmology and the other co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. “Lessons learned from these infrequent, late-onset genetic eye diseases offer glimpses at possible mechanisms of disease for much more frequent retinal problems.”

title: A New Fiber Supplement Could Be a Game Changer for Millions With IBS
content:
Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a common gastrointestinal disorder that affects how the intestines function. It can cause abdominal pain, bloating, gas, diarrhea, and constipation, with symptoms varying from person to person. Credit: Shutterstock
For people with IBS, a specially designed fiber blend could support a healthier gut without added pain or bloating, a trial alongside a low-FODMAP diet suggests.
Cutting out foods that leave you bloated or in pain can bring welcome relief. For millions of people with irritable bowel syndrome, or IBS, however, a diet that eases discomfort can come with a trade-off. Restricting certain foods can also reduce fiber intake and the beneficial bacteria that help support gut health.
Researchers at Edith Cowan University (ECU) in Australia have tested a specially formulated fiber blend that could help address that dilemma. Called ur gut, the supplement combines high-amylose maize resistant starch with psyllium husk powder. In a small clinical trial, the blend changed the composition of participants’ gut bacteria without worsening their abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, or constipation.
Low-FODMAP diets can reduce beneficial bacteria
IBS is common worldwide and affects nearly 11 percent of Australians. Its cause remains unknown, although stress, infection, and medication are potential triggers. Certain foods, poor sleep, psychological stress, hormonal fluctuations, and lifestyle factors can aggravate symptoms.
One common recommendation is a low-FODMAP diet, which limits certain carbohydrates that gut bacteria readily ferment.
“For years we’ve known that a diet low in fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols (FODMAPs) can relieve symptoms, but they can also reduce beneficial gut bacteria and negatively impact fiber intake over time,” said lead author Dr. Tina Yan.
“We wanted to find a way to build better gut health while following a low-FODMAP diet.”
Fiber reshaped gut bacteria without worsening IBS
Scientists at ECU’s Nutrition and Health Innovation Research Institute (NHIRI) developed the blend and trialed it in people with IBS who were following a low-FODMAP diet. Adding fiber in this setting requires care because bacteria can produce gas as they break it down.
“Traditionally, fermentable fibers can be difficult for people with IBS because they can increase gas production and discomfort,” Dr. Yan said.
“What’s exciting about this study is that participants maintained stable symptoms while showing meaningful improvements in their gut microbiota as well as in their gut-related anxiety.”
The changes in participants’ gut bacterial composition were significant, and their extent stood out to ur gut® co-creator Professor Amanda Devine.
“Changes of this magnitude are rarely seen with such a short intervention,” she said.
“The study demonstrated that our targeted dietary fiber blend positively reshaped the gut microbiome in people with IBS following a low-FODMAP diet, supporting beneficial bacteria linked to gut and mental health. This was great to see.”
How two fibers may support gut health
The researchers suspect the explanation lies in how the blend’s two ingredients, resistant starch and psyllium husk, work together. Resistant starch escapes digestion in the small intestine, leaving it available for bacteria to ferment in the colon. Psyllium appears to slow that fermentation, allowing the starch to travel farther into the colon before bacteria break it down. The researchers believe this enhances the production of beneficial metabolites, substances the bacteria produce as they process the starch.
“For many people with IBS, success has traditionally meant simply avoiding certain foods,” said ur gut® co-creator Associate Professor Claus Christophersen.
“Our findings suggest we may also be able to actively rebuild gut health and the microbiome while not making IBS symptoms worse. That’s an important step forward.”

Dunican, Kanita Kunaratnam, Lesley Andrew and Claus T. Christophersen, 24 September 2026,
European Journal of Nutrition

title: Could a Nasal Spray Stop Alzheimer’s Before Memory Loss Begins?
content:
Scientists have developed an experimental nasal spray that protects crucial brain connections and improves memory in animal models of Alzheimer’s disease. Credit: Shutterstock
Protecting memory from Alzheimer’s may one day involve a nasal spray, with encouraging results in animals and evidence that its particles also protect human neurons grown in the lab.
Alzheimer’s disease damages the connections that allow brain cells to communicate, threatening memory. A nasal spray containing tiny particles naturally released by cells has helped protect those connections in an animal model of the disease. The treatment both prevented memory deficits and countered cognitive decline after it had begun.
The particles, called extracellular vesicles, are small packages that cells release into their surroundings. Those used in this study came from cells of the amniotic membrane, the tissue lining the sac that surrounds a developing fetus. Researchers at the Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Fondazione Policlinico Universitario A. Gemelli IRCCS, and the E. Menni Research Center of Fondazione Poliambulanza reported the findings in
Translational Neurodegeneration
When administered through the nose to animals that mimic features of Alzheimer’s disease, the vesicles reached the hippocampus, a brain region crucial for memory and particularly vulnerable to the disease. There, they entered both neurons and microglia, cells that monitor conditions in the brain and help defend it. The treatment counteracted neuroinflammation and protected neuronal function, particularly at synapses, the connections through which nerve cells transmit information. These effects were accompanied by a significant improvement in cognitive abilities.
The choice of amniotic membrane cells grew out of years of placental research by Professor Ornella Parolini, a full professor of applied biology and scientific director of IRCCS Ospedale “Casa Sollievo della sofferenza.” Her work has focused on these cells and the substances they release, collectively known as the secretome, investigating their protective and regenerative effects in various experimental models. The E. Menni Research Center, led by Parolini, contributed expertise in isolating and characterizing the cells and identifying the molecules they produce.
The research combined the expertise of Professor Claudio Grassi, whose team at the Università Cattolica studies brain inflammation and plasticity, with work by Professor Salvatore Fusco on the vesicles’ effects in the brain. Lead authors Dr. Andrea Papait and Dr. Francesca Natale helped connect these findings, investigating how amniotic extracellular vesicles influence brain inflammation, neuronal function, and memory.
The findings also suggest that effective Alzheimer’s treatments may need to address more than the buildup of harmful proteins in the brain.
Professor Fusco explains: “The study suggests the need to direct research into Alzheimer’s therapies by focusing not only on counteracting the accumulation of toxic compounds like beta-amyloid and tau, but also by paying close attention to the cellular environment in which neurons live (e.g., microglia and astrocytes) and the molecular signals (e.g., cytokines or microRNAs) exchanged by these cells, which can influence synapse function.”
Protection extends to laboratory-grown human neurons
To investigate the protective effects in human cells, researchers used skin biopsies collected from patients with Alzheimer’s disease and healthy individuals at the Policlinico’s Memory Clinic. From those samples, they generated pluripotent stem cells, which can develop into different cell types, and then used those cells to produce human neurons.
The vesicles also showed protective effects in these laboratory-grown neurons, extending the evidence to experimental human models and giving the study a closer connection to patients.
Professor Grassi emphasizes that the findings are encouraging but still preliminary.
“These are preclinical results that require further validation in humans and do not yet represent an available therapy for Alzheimer’s disease, but they point to a very promising direction: understanding whether some of the mechanisms through which the placenta naturally regulates inflammation and protects tissues could offer new tools for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases and, more generally, whether the use of extracellular vesicles represents a new frontier for the treatment of neurological diseases.”
Reference: “Human amniotic mesenchymal stromal cell-derived extracellular vesicles reprogram microglia and prevent neurodegeneration in experimental models of Alzheimer’s disease” by Andrea Papait, Francesca Natale, Antonietta Rosa Silini, Ida Nifo Sarrapochiello, Elisa Orecchini, Raimondo Sollazzo, Marco Rinaudo, Serafina Farigu, Nicoletta Garofalo, Giulia Mantini, Guido Maria Giuffrè, Pietro Romele, Elvira Ragozzino, Alice Dellaria, Luciano Giacò, Camillo Marra, Cristian Ripoli, Claudio Grassi, Ornella Parolini and Salvatore Fusco, 9 September 2026,

title: PeroCycle and Glass Futures plan two-tonne pilot reactor for perovskite-based CO₂ recycling
content:
PeroCycle and Glass Futures plan two-tonne pilot reactor for perovskite-based CO₂ recycling
PeroCycle
, a University of Birmingham spin-out developing perovskite-catalyst carbon recycling, says its memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Glass Futures will lead to a two-tonne pilot reactor at Glass Futures’ site in St Helens, Merseyside. The partners plan to test the reactor throughout 2027. The MoU was first announced in September as an agreement to evaluate a collaboration over a six-month period.
Glass Futures plant in St Helens, Merseyside.
PeroCycle’s technology uses a perovskite catalyst to split carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide at lower temperatures than conventional methods, and recycles the CO into industrial processes as a feedstock. The company says it could cut emissions from foundation industries such as steelmaking by up to 90%. The catalyst has been validated in the laboratory, but the company says it now needs to validate both the catalyst and the reactor in high-temperature industrial conditions.
Under the MoU, Glass Futures will provide a clean and varied gas supply for the tests, and PeroCycle’s catalyst can be produced on site using Glass Futures’ material blending and furnace facilities. The partners will also set up systems to scale catalyst manufacturing from the laboratory to pilot scale. PeroCycle CEO Grant Budge said the lab prototype demonstrated performance in optimal conditions, and that the company will also benchmark and review the catalyst’s formulation and structure.
PeroCycle has also been named to the 2026 Cleantech 50 to Watch list, as one of three companies recognized for heavy-industry decarbonization and the only one from the UK.

title: Japan’s iodine producers expand output, with perovskite solar cells in view
content:
Japan’s iodine producers expand output, with perovskite solar cells in view
Chiba Prefecture, which accounts for about 80% of Japan’s iodine production, is looking to perovskite solar cells as a source of future demand, according to a recent report. Iodine is one of the main ingredients of perovskite solar cells, and Japan is the world’s second-largest iodine producer after Chile. The iodine is extracted from brine groundwater in the South Kanto Gas Field, which lies beneath Chiba. Production is centered on the Kujukuri area. The report says that demand for medical iodine is already rising, particularly in Asia, and that the spread of perovskite solar cells is expected to boost it further.
Producers in the prefecture are investing to expand.
ISE Chemicals
, which the report says holds about 10% of global iodine production, is investing more than 10 billion yen (about US$63 million) through 2028, partly to upgrade plant equipment in Chiba. The company is also starting full-scale iodine production in the US, and plans to increase its annual output from about 4,000 tons to about 7,500 tons by the end of 2030. K&O Iodine aims to raise its annual output from about 1,650 tons to more than 2,000 tons in the 2030s, and Godo Shigen plans to add 300 tons of recycled iodine over the next three years.
Increasing output is not simple. Pumping large volumes of brine can cause ground subsidence, so the amount of surface drainage is limited area by area. Producers have agreed with the prefectural government to return water underground after extracting gas and iodine, but an industry source told the newspaper that the ground is too firm for water to penetrate easily, and that output cannot rise quickly without technological innovation. Godo Shigen’s president, Yasuhiko Otani, said the company hopes to account for new demand with aggressive capital investment.
The report also notes that a three-year demonstration test of film-type perovskite solar cells over a rice paddy has begun at Chiba University’s Kashiwanoha Campus, to study power generation efficiency and the effect on rice yields. It cites research firm Fuji Keizai, which expects the global perovskite solar cell market to grow 2.3 times to 108.8 billion yen (about US$689 million) in 2026, and to reach 3.69 trillion yen (about US$23 billion) in 2040.

title: Atomic-scale imaging reveals polar nanodomains in CsPbI₃ perovskite
content:
Atomic-scale imaging reveals polar nanodomains in CsPbI₃ perovskite
Researchers from Monash University and the University of Oxford have directly observed local, ferroelectric-like polarization at twin walls inside CsPbI₃, a halide perovskite that is centrosymmetric and nonpolar overall.
Whether photoactive halide perovskites show useful ferroelectric behavior, and whether it could be used to boost the performance of solar cells through the bulk photovoltaic effect, has been under debate. To look for an answer, the team used low-dose scanning transmission electron microscopy to image vapor-deposited CsPbI₃ thin films at the atomic scale. The approach limits damage to the beam-sensitive material.
The researchers identified ferroelastic twin walls parallel to {110} and {112} planes. At the {110} twin walls, they observed lead atoms shifting position, which drives a local ferroelectric-like polarization. The team says these polar walls, which are confined to a few atomic layers, form an intrinsic array of nanoscale interfaces spaced about 30 to 50 nm apart within the otherwise nonpolar lattice. The university says the lead atoms are displaced by about 15 picometers and that the polar regions are roughly four atomic layers wide.
The {112} twin walls behave differently. They show no polar displacement of lead, but strongly suppress octahedral tilt and the off-center displacement of cesium atoms, which the researchers describe as a different structural degree of freedom that has not yet been exploited.
The authors suggest the findings point to opportunities for enhanced conductivity and photovoltaic behavior through domain wall engineering, analogous to approaches used in oxide ferroics. The work is at the materials-characterization stage, and the paper does not report device results.

content:
11月3日至5日，第二届先进储能技术及应用挑战赛在南京举行。作为CESC2026第四届储能大会暨储能及智能电网设备应用展览会的重要组成部分，本届挑战赛在三天内完成了从现场实测、奖项评定到成果路演的全流程：11月3日至4日，九大赛道同台竞技；11月4日晚，颁奖典礼揭晓27项获奖成果；11月5日上午，获奖项目集中路演，与金融资本、能源投资、政府产业孵化三个方向的专家组现场对接。
一场赛事，既回答了“技术怎么评”，也回答了“成果怎么落”。

11月3日至4日，现场实测与项目评比同步展开。参赛项目不再依赖单方送样或书面材料，而是在同一工况条件、同一时间窗口内接受多方交叉验证——这也是本届赛事与常规行业评比最大的不同。

11月4日晚，挑战赛颁奖典礼举行，27项获奖成果集中揭晓。
经过现场实测与专家评审，第二届先进储能技术及应用挑战赛各奖项评选结果揭晓。
先锋奖授予在系统方案与产业落地方面具有示范引领作用的项目。获奖成果包括：中钠能源（扬州）聚阴离子型钠离子储能电芯及系统解决方案，江苏珈云新材料新能源电池高性能气凝胶技术，南京和本机电设备储能PACK极早期火灾预警系统，西安汇川技术IES600系列125kW储能变流器，以及河海大学新能源学院AI驱动储能经济测算及优化运行平台等。北京寄云鼎城、库柏（宁波）电气、无锡申泰新能源、天际装备科技（苏州）、玉柴芯蓝（江苏）氢能源、江苏元感微电子、厦门新能集智控、智储微网（江苏）培训中心等单位的成果同时获奖。
创新奖授予在现场测试中展现较高技术水准的技术路线型项目，包括：中储国能（北京）300MW级先进压缩空气储能技术，南京南瑞继保电气非洲凯鹏矿业新能源电力系统，中科南京未来能源系统研究院高性能固态储氢材料与装备，以及东南大学机械工程学院复合材料高压储氢气瓶安全原位监测技术等。南京锂泰新能源、协鑫新能源运营科技、江苏维锂能源、懿朵智慧声谷（南通）、厦门新能集智控、中国电子科技集团第五十五研究所等单位的成果同获该奖。
领先奖与卓越奖授予各项实测指标表现卓越的项目。吉钠（江苏）科技、江苏众钠能源、兆钠新能源、新能量（江苏）能源科技四家单位凭借钠离子电池低温性能、循环寿命与系统集成等方面的突出表现获奖。
其中，新能量（江苏）能源科技有限公司共有7项技术获奖，涵盖钠电池高安全无感投切台区储能设备、模块化可移动光储柴微电网集成技术与系统等，是本届挑战赛获奖项目最多的单位。
特别贡献奖授予为赛事评审与行业生态建设作出突出贡献的专家，裴哲义、周锡卫、唐西胜、郑杰允、郭鹏宇、吉立东、周喜超、马歆八位专家获奖。
国际友谊奖授予推动国际储能合作、莅临本届大会参观交流的国际友人，澳大利亚中国工商业委员会Frank Mcguire获奖。
奖项揭晓并非终点。颁奖次日，主办方即组织获奖项目与投资机构、产业主体现场对接，推动优秀成果加快转化落地。
三、获奖项目集中路演，三类专家现场对接
11月5日上午，第二届先进储能技术及应用挑战赛获奖项目集中路演在CESC2026第四届储能大会暨展览会5号馆举行，这是本届挑战赛的最后一环。来自金融资本、能源投资、政府产业孵化三个方向的专家组到场听会，与参赛单位围绕关键指标、实测数据与落地条件展开对接。
储能技术从实验室走向市场，要跨过融资、工程与落地三道门槛，任何单一环节都无法独立完成对接。本届路演首次按资本属性组织专家组，把金融资本、能源投资与政府产业孵化三类主体请到同一场，让参赛项目在同一时间、同一场所分别回答融资可行性、工程经济性与落地条件三方面的问题，三个方向各有分工、互为补充。
金融资本专家组由银行、融资租赁、私募基金、券商系资本等机构组成。工商银行南京分行深度参与本届储能大会，发挥科技金融、绿色金融优势，为储能行业创新发展注入金融活水。参与本组听会的还包括南通国润融资租赁、河北省金融租赁、华夏银行南京分行、交通银行/交银资本、宁波银行南京分行、兴业银行、浙商银行南京分行、徽商银行南京分行、杭州银行南京大厂支行、兴业证券江苏分公司、兴证创新资本、毅达资本、咏圣资本、国联金投致源（江苏）私募基金、南京辰光投资管理等机构代表。这一组关注的是项目的融资结构、投贷联动与风险分担，回答"钱从哪里来"。
能源投资专家组由能源央企、地方能源集团、电力建设与设计单位、新能源投资运营企业组成，包括中国能源建设集团江苏省电力建设第一工程有限公司、国家电投集团江苏新能源有限公司、华润电力投资有限公司华东分公司、华润电力南京公司、扬州市能源投资发展集团、无锡市创新投资集团、常州绿色能源（常州能源集团）、南京能网云创新能源科技（南京新能源产业集团）、中能国新产业投资（南京）集团、江苏绿发投资、中建六局建设发展、中建八局第三建设、南京南瑞继保电气、江苏沿海易碳数字科技、江苏沿海碳资产管理等企业代表。这一组关注的是技术方案的工程可行性、全生命周期成本与收益模型，回答"项目能不能建、建成划不划算"。
政府产业孵化专家组由省内外工信主管部门、开发区与园区管委会、招商投促机构组成，包括南京市、无锡市、淮安市、宿迁市、泰州市、盐城市、南通市、连云港市工业和信息化局，南京市鼓楼区投资促进局、南京鼓楼高新区管委会、江苏如东洋口港经济开发区管委会、盐城绿色低碳科创园，以及镇江市发展和改革委员会、衢州市招商投资促进中心、包头招商投促局、金湖县政府驻南京招商办等单位代表。这一组关注的是项目落地所需的载体条件、要素保障与产业配套，回答"项目往哪里落"。
路演现场，获奖单位围绕各赛道核心指标作汇报。据组委会介绍，参与路演的获奖项目覆盖从电芯材料、核心设备到系统集成、场景应用的主要环节，其中既有面向电网侧调峰调频、构网型支撑的系统级方案，也有面向钠离子电池产业化、压缩空气储能、氢储能全产业链的技术路线成果，还有面向零碳园区、算力中心、新能源船舶等新兴场景的应用方案。
四、检测认证前置，实测数据可追溯可复核
路演之所以能谈得具体，底气来自赛场上的实测数据。
与一般项目路演不同，此次汇报的技术参数均来自赛场实测：可现场实测的项目，实测结果须不低于现行国家标准；暂无国家标准的，由专家组按行业标准制定实测门槛。技术成色不再由企业自己说了算。
本届挑战赛把检测认证环节前置到比赛现场，由中电智慧储能科技（上海）、南京市产品质量监督检验院（国家智能电网应用产品质量检验检测中心）、中电联（北京）电力检测技术研究院、国家高端储能产品质量检验检测中心（江苏）等机构专家同步实测，联合鉴证数据真实性并共同签发实测证书。这一安排使得参赛项目在进入路演环节时，已具备可追溯、可复核的数据基础。
对投资方而言，实测数据降低了技术判断的不确定性；对参赛单位而言，一次实测形成的数据可同时用于项目评审、融资尽调与业主选型，一次投入、多处复用。
五、以赛促产，让技术成果走向落地
路演现场，多家参赛单位与投资机构、能源企业就后续测试、试点与商务合作进行了初步沟通。
组委会方面表示，挑战赛将继续以真实工况、真实数据检验技术水平，把赛事形成的实测数据与技术评价结果，转化为产业链协同与项目落地的实际支撑，服务新型电力系统建设与储能产业高质量发展。
从现场实测到奖项揭晓，从集中路演到资源对接——三天时间，这场赛事完成了一次技术评价与产业转化的完整闭环。奖牌是终点，也是起点。

title: 九载全勤 未来共进 GE Vernova以
content:
作为进博会九年"全勤生"，GE Vernova持续深化植根中国承诺，以"能源变革之力"赋能中国能源转型
与北京大学能源研究院联合发布《中国绿氢燃机应用与展望》
亚洲首秀低碳能源转型沙盘，中国首秀GRiDEA低碳环保电网解决方案及沉浸式虚拟现实体验区，带来GCB发电机断路器模型，展示多款主力燃机模型及低碳解决方案
与山东电力建设第三工程有限公司签署马来西亚玻璃州新建IPP联合循环燃气轮机项目EPC 合同；与中国华电集团有限公司签署两项服务合作协议
上海2026年11月6日 /美通社/ -- 11月5日-10日，第九届中国国际进口博览会（以下简称"进博会"）在上海隆重举办，GE Vernova以"能源变革之力"为主题再赴进博之约。作为进博会九年"全勤生"，GE Vernova持续为中国市场引入前沿理念、提供技术与服务，携手各方合作伙伴赋能中国能源转型、助力中国新型电力系统建设。
GE Vernova第九届进博会展台
"亚洲首秀"、"中国首秀"领衔，全面演绎"能源变革之力"
本届展会上，GE Vernova 带来了低碳能源转型沙盘、GCB 发电机断路器模型、GRiDEA低碳环保电网解决方案、沉浸式虚拟现实体验区、多款主力燃机机型模型以及低碳解决方案，从系统方案、电网产品到发电设备，完整呈现其面向新型电力系统的技术布局。
作为展台一大亮点，全新升级的低碳能源转型沙盘迎来"亚洲首秀"。沙盘聚焦西北大基地、中部地区、东南沿海三大场景，系统地呈现中国不同区域资源禀赋下的低碳能源方案，展现了燃机的多元场景应用，通过风、光、绿氢、燃机的深度耦合，不仅消纳绿氢、提供稳定电力，更在可再生能源出力波动时发挥关键调峰作用，支撑电网稳定。
低碳能源转型沙盘
在电网解决方案领域，GE Vernova在本届进博会上带来了GCB发电机断路器模型。发电机断路器广泛应用于各种形式的发电厂，安装在发电机和升压变之间，可及时切断短路电流，保护发电机和变压器等关键设备。GE Vernova已有超过300台发电机断路器稳定运行于各种形式的电厂，近年来其更广泛应用于F级和HA级别大型燃气燃机联合循环发电项目。
同一展区，GE Vernova还展出了"中国首秀"的去SF₆技术——这也是GE Vernova GRiDEA低碳环保电网解决方案的一部分，能提供与SF₆开关设备相当的可靠性，同时在设备全生命周期内显著降低碳足迹。目前，GE Vernova的去SF₆解决方案已经覆盖到电网各电压等级的全系列高压开关产品，其无SF₆产品已被140余家领先电网运营商选用，并在欧美地区的骨干电网中得到广泛应用。
展台的另一处亮点，是"中国首秀"的沉浸式虚拟现实体验区——"从分子到能源"，以第一人称视角展示燃气发电等不同发电形式从燃料或自然能源到能源转换、电力输送、最终服务日常生活的完整过程，帮助与会来宾和观众身临其境地感受电力生产的完整过程。
在燃机设备方面，三款主力机型同台亮相。9HA燃机集先进、高效、低碳、可靠等诸多优势于一身，适合在大城市集群用作纯凝发电，作为调峰机组与可再生能源进行互补。截至2026年5月，其全球商业运行时间已突破400万小时，在中国市场更收获6个项目、共13台机组，装机容量突破970万千瓦，预计和同等规模燃煤机组相比每年减排二氧化碳超1050万吨。
6F.03燃机在同等级别的F级燃机中，以发电效率高、应用多样以及运行可靠等优势，在热电联供和分布式能源应用中尤为亮眼，已在中国收获50台订单，其中47台燃机已投入商业运营，成为10万千瓦等级分布式能源项目的理想选择。
LM6000 VELOX航改型燃机基于成熟航空技术，拥有高效率、高可靠性、高可利用率、低排放等特点，具备100%燃氢发电能力，主要应用于灵活性电力支持、调峰、电网稳固服务、热电联产、分布式能源。该机型拥有快速启动和燃料灵活性的优势，冷态启动仅需5分钟即可达到满负荷运行，并支持多种燃料的灵活使用与在线燃料切换。
在低碳技术领域，展台集中呈现了直接空气捕获技术（DAC）模型与燃机联合循环电厂碳捕获解决方案（CCS）模型。直接空气捕获技术实现了从大气中直接捕获二氧化碳的突破，其可重复使用的DAC模块制造过程简化，组装过程便捷，同时易于维护，且服务方便。碳捕获解决方案具备卓越的高效减排能力，并在助力电厂降低碳排放的同时减少对效率和出力的影响，为联合循环发电厂提供高达95%碳捕获效率的解决方案。
重磅报告发布，携各方探索绿氢燃机未来
当前，全国可再生能源发展迅速，对电力系统调节能力提出了更高要求，而绿氢燃机是满足这一需求的可行方案之一。进博会期间，GE Vernova联合北京大学能源研究院共同发布《中国绿氢燃机应用与展望》。报告聚焦将绿电转化为氢，在需要时通过燃机发电，为新型能源体系建设和能源转型进程提供可行路径的探索。
《中国绿氢燃机应用与展望》发布
北京大学能源研究院副院长杨雷表示："绿氢燃机是把风光资源转化为系统级可靠电力的重要技术，报告为产业落地提供了共识路径；对中国而言，绿氢作为长时间大规模的储能方式，已经不是能源转型中的一种可选技术，而是必须提前布局的战略选择。此次报告的发布，为绿氢燃机发电应用的落地指明了方向，也为新型电力系统建设提供了前瞻参考，期待各方齐心聚力共同推进绿氢燃机行业的高质量发展。"
北京大学能源研究院副院长杨雷
通用电气能源投资（中国）有限公司董事长许欣表示："GE Vernova以安全、可靠、可负担、可持续的电力供应，为能源转型提供有力支持。中国拥有全球最大的可再生能源装机规模，和全球最具竞争力的绿电制氢的工业生态体系，这使中国成为全球有望率先实现绿氢在发电领域大规模应用的国家。我们期待与中国伙伴一起，让绿氢燃机从示范走向商业化应用，把尚未被充分利用的风光资源转化为系统需要的稳定电力。进博会始终是我们贴近中国市场、服务本地客户的重要平台。未来，我们期待与中国伙伴同频共进，让GE Vernova的技术和解决方案持续创造价值，为中国的能源转型进程提供切实支撑，助力'双碳'目标和高质量发展。"
通用电气能源投资（中国）有限公司董事长许欣
一直以来，GE Vernova不断探索氢气等新燃料的应用可能性，旗下燃机已具备不同比例氢气燃烧的能力。例如，LM6000 VELOX航改型燃机具备100%燃氢发电能力；LM2500航改型燃机具备高达85%的氢气燃烧能力；9HA.01、9HA.02重型燃机具备50%掺氢燃烧能力。
九赴进博之约，坚守植根中国承诺
进博会不仅是前沿技术展示与行业交流的舞台，更是合作成果落地的重要平台。本届进博会上，GE Vernova与山东电力建设第三工程有限公司就马来西亚玻璃州的新建IPP（独立发电商）联合循环燃气轮机项目签署EPC合同。项目将配备一台GE Vernova 9HA.02燃气轮机及配套发电机，电厂计划于2029年投入运行。随着东南亚迈入经济与工业增长的新阶段，该项目将为这一进程贡献力量，同时助力该地区建设更具韧性的能源未来。该合同的签订也标志着GE Vernova与山东电力建设第三工程有限公司长期合作的又一里程碑——双方将先进燃气轮机技术与成熟的EPC能力相结合，为区域发展注入动力。
此外，GE Vernova 还与中国华电集团有限公司签署了两项服务合作协议。根据协议，GE Vernova将向华电集团提供9E燃气轮机备件及服务，助力其旗下相关燃机机组的可靠运行；同时，GE Vernova与华电通用轻型燃机设备有限公司再度携手，将为华润电力（常州）有限公司的2台LM6000PF航改型燃机提供维修服务，涵盖机组维修、热部套及燃烧室部件更换。此次签约是 GE Vernova在华服务能力的又一落地，标志着双方在服务领域的合作持续深化。

政策分类依据: ‘十五五’规划提出2030年风光高峰供电占比超20%等定量目标与时间表
content:
11月6日，国家发展改革委召开“奋进‘十五五’”系列新闻发布会的第三场，介绍筑牢安全底座有关情况。
会上，国家能源局发展规划司副司长葛炬表示，今年迎峰度夏期间，全国用电负荷4次刷新历史极值，最大值比去年增加5000万千瓦，华北、东北、华东等6个区域电网用电负荷23次创新高，我国电力系统平稳运行，有力保障了全社会生产生活用电需求。
“十五五”时期，在算力等新兴产业带动下，我国用电需求仍将刚性增长，预计年均增量将达到6000亿度左右，相当于每年新增3个上海市的用电量。为做好电力保供，我们建立了电力供应充裕度预警机制，提出2030年电力供应充裕度大于1.1，也就是在用电负荷最高峰时刻，仍然有10%的保供能力余量，确保关键时刻能够“顶住峰、兜住底”。具体来说，将从源网荷储协同发力，加强电力保供能力建设。
在电源侧，一手抓传统电源兜底保障，实施新一代煤电改造升级，推动煤电向支撑性调节性电源转型。因地制宜布局一批调峰气电。有序推进水电、核电重大工程建设。另一手抓新能源安全可靠替代，持续提升新能源发电功率预测精度，布局建设一批系统友好型新能源电站，重点增强可靠顶峰发电能力。到2030年，在迎峰度夏、迎峰度冬晚高峰等电力保供压力最大的时段，风电、光伏为系统贡献的发电量占比达到20%以上、提高约10个百分点。
在电网侧，加快建设主配微协同的新型电网，充分发挥我国大电网“全国一盘棋”的优势，加强西电东送能力建设，推动省间电力互补互济能力提升4000万千瓦，打造坚强韧性的配电系统，增强配电网供电保障能力和综合承载力，提升智能微电网自平衡、自调节能力。
在用户侧，充分挖掘电动汽车、空调等电力负荷调节潜力，全面推广智能有序充电，扩大车网互动规模化应用范围，促进虚拟电厂规模化发展，推动2030年虚拟电厂调节能力达到5000万千瓦以上，让用户更多参与电力系统调节互动。
在储能侧，更好发挥储能作为电力系统“充电宝”、“调节器”的作用，合理布局建设一批抽水蓄能电站，2030年装机规模达到1.6亿千瓦左右。大力发展新型储能，鼓励多种技术路线发展，2030年装机规模达到3亿千瓦。
另外，近年来极端天气频发强发，面对超强厄尔尼诺可能带来的影响，我们将加强电力供需形势分析研判，强化监测预警和应急管控，以安全充裕的电力供应体系，有效应对各种不确定性。

title: Construction completed for Baltyk 2 and 3 base
content:
Construction of an operations and maintenance (O&M) base to support
the Baltyk
and Baltyk 3 offshore wind farms has been officially completed.
Located in Leba, the facility has received its occupancy permit and has
been handed over to Equinor, which is developing the projects alongside
Polenergia. According to the announcement, Equinor will be responsible
for the operations and maintenance of both offshore wind farms.
Baltyk 2 and Baltyk 3 will each have an installed capacity of 720 MW and
are scheduled to enter operation in 2027. Together with the planned Baltyk
1 project, the three wind farms will form the Baltyk Offshore Wind Farm
portfolio, which is expected to deliver a combined installed capacity of
up to 3 GW, enough to supply renewable electricity to more than 4 million
households.
The O&M base will serve as a hub for offshore technicians and teams
responsible for coordinating and supporting marine operations. The base
includes office and staff facilities, a remote operations and control centre
for the wind farms, a spare-parts warehouse, and infrastructure designed
to support marine activities.
The base has also been designed with sustainability in mind. To help reduce
its environmental impact, the facility incorporates photovoltaic panels,
heat pumps, heat recovery ventilation systems, and a rainwater collection
and reuse system.

title: ORLEN Neptun launches Baltic West wind measurement campaign
content:
ORLEN Neptun has announced that its Baltic
West offshore wind farm
has begun a certified wind measurement campaign, marking a key milestone
in the project's development.
The Baltic West project comprises four areas located on the Oder Bank and
will have a total installed capacity of 4 GW, enough to power more than
5 million Polish households.
The campaign is being carried out by Partrac, Venterra Group’s specialist
metocean and seabed consultancy, which will apply its V-LiDAR technology.
According to the announcement, the launch brings the project one step closer
to participating in Poland's offshore wind auction, which is currently
scheduled for 2027.
As part of the campaign, two V-LiDAR buoy systems will be deployed to provide
precise, validated data to support the project's development, helping to
reduce both project data and offshore health and safety risks.
Marcin Sowiñski, Baltic West Project Director, said: "The launch of
the wind measurement campaign is another key step in bringing the Baltic
West project closer to collecting the complete set of data needed to develop
a financial model."
Adding: "We will be able to base further decisions on actual, verified
measurement data rather than on assumptions or estimates."

export cable infrastructure, known as Cambois Connection, in English waters.

onshore at Cambois, supporting the 4.1GW Berwick Bank Wind Farm, which

Scottish Government ministers approved the wind farm's array infrastructure
in July 2025, while consent for the Cambois Connection infrastructure in
English waters followed in August.

third phase of the Berwick Bank project. Once completed, the export cable
infrastructure is expected to provide up to 1.8GW of transmission capacity.
Iain Jarvie, Berwick Bank C Senior Project Manager at SSE Renewables, said:
“Together with the consent already secured for the onshore infrastructure
in Northumberland, this decision provides further momentum and reflects
the continued progress being made across the Berwick Bank development.”

title: Nvidia Drama Explodes; The Startup Tricking Scammers by Using AI Agents
content: Shares of Nvidia were trading down 5% early Monday morning, a sign of the huge uncertainty now hanging over the AI chip giant in the wake of the company’s disclosure Sunday that it would investigate recent reporting that CEO Jensen Huang “had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” Adding to the drama, Huang acknowledged having had an affair, saying he was “deeply sorry.” The New York Times reported last month that Huang had a “close relationship” with a Chinese businesswoman who allegedly shared intelligence with Beijing authorities. We don’t know where this will lead. But given Huang’s position as one of AI’s biggest advocates, the ripples could be felt everywhere in the sector. Meanwhile, an Australian startup has come up with a new way to fight AI-enabled cybercrimes: sending an army of AI agents to pose as gullible grandmas and unsuspecting job seekers so as to lure the bad guys. Apate.ai is going up against a multibillion-dollar scam industry powered by thousands of workers in scam compounds, mostly in Southeast Asia. These scammers have gotten more sophisticated with the help of technology. Investigators have struggled to keep pace with ever-evolving tactics, and often only begin the chase after victims report their losses. Apate.ai, founded in 2024, thinks it’s found a way to help tip the scales. By posing as potential victims, its army of AI agents are able to engage scammers in lengthy conversations designed partly to waste time and divert attention from real victims. But it’s not just about wasting their time. In these conversations, Apate.ai extracts vital intelligence about syndicates. Everything from the scammers’ bank accounts, crypto wallet addresses and conversation metadata are used by telecommunication companies, banks and government agencies to help triangulate suspicious calls or to target criminal networks. Scammers encounter Apate.ai’s agents through two ways, co-founder and chief product officer Peter Eckermann said in an interview.  When a scammer calls a grandma, the call may get flagged by the telco based on several data points, including an abnormal volume of calls originating from the number over short periods. That‘s when the call gets blocked and diverted to an AI agent. One of Apate.ai’s biggest customers, TPG Telecom , a leading telco in Australia, has diverted around 590,000 calls to Apate.ai’s bots. The second way is when agents engage with scam ads, infiltrate dodgy WhatsApp investment groups or interact with websites containing malicious links. Apate.ai estimates its agents have engaged with scammers across 57.5 million interactions with an accumulative time of 27 years. Apate.ai is in the U.S. but now plans to expand its operations here, where cybercrime is widespread. The State Department estimates that Americans lost at least $18.2 billion to scam centers in Southeast Asia in 2025. Eckermann is relocating from Australia to lead the expansion efforts, after the startup raised $8.15 million in seed funding led by Palo Alto, Calif.-based Lobby Capital . It previously raised 2.5 million Australian dollars ($1.7 million) led by Australian venture capital firm OIF Ventures, announced in August 2025. Much of the startup’s recent research has focused on getting its agents to retain context, better analyze adversarial environments where scammers are present, and engage longer with fraudsters without breaking persona. “It gives us the upper hand mathematically when we're engaging with a threat actor using AI,” Eckermann said. Scambaiting—beating fraudsters at their own game—isn’t new. Internet vigilantes have been working on it for years. But the use of agentic AI to combat scam on a large scale has been slow, as a bulk of funding and resources have poured into hot startups working on agents for coding, productivity and lifestyle. Apate.ai, named after the Greek goddess of deceit, started as a research project in Macquarie University in Sydney. Dali Kaafar , the startup’s CEO and a computer science professor, strung a research team together in 2021 after he was inspired by his 44-minute prank call with an obvious scammer. The team modeled the stages of a conversation using probability theory by analyzing close to 1,700 hours of YouTube videos of people conversing. They spoke to scambaiters to understand the flow of conversations with fraudsters. Kaafar and his fellow researchers also delved into how well large language models could craft victim personas while remaining coherent. Last year, they published research that evaluated 3,200 simulated dialogues, and found that GPT-4 performed particularly well on conversational naturalness and believable personas, while DeepSeek-R1 sustained longer engagements. (Both OpenAI and DeepSeek have since released newer models.) Apate.ai uses its own fine-tuned model trained on conversations its agents have had with scammers and material from Kaafar’s research. It also uses a mix of frontier and open-weight models to generate outputs, such as realistic screenshots containing a victim’s personal information. It uses ElevenLabs for voice synthesis, and Cloudflare’s Clef decision models, which classify the information an agent encounters, helping it decide how to act. Eckermann said the Clef system has helped the company extract insights more efficiently without a massive cost of compute. Apate.ai is experimenting with Chinese open-weight models, in particular the GLM models from Z.ai . The company hasn’t used any yet, as it is testing the models’ performance in various use cases. “If we are doing work in the U.S., where there are restrictions within particular agencies around what models are used, we need to be careful from that perspective too,” Eckermann said. Nvidia’s board announced Sunday it was launching an investigation into Huang as well. Unity shares have rallied nearly 200% since March. OpenAI is expected to host a call with investors next week to discuss its third-quarter results, according to a person familiar with the plan. The discussions follow the close of the first part of its latest round, which raised $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation before the investment. title: Meta Plans Sales Team, Consulting Partnerships to Win Over Big Companies
content: Meta Platforms is taking the next steps in a plan to build a new business selling its AI products to companies. The company has begun forming a sales organization to sell those products to small and midsize businesses and also forge relationships with consulting firms and systems integrators, including Accenture, Deloitte and IBM, to help it sell and deploy AI products to corporate customers, according to a person familiar with the matter and job postings reviewed by The Information. The efforts are a key part of Meta’s plan to turn its massive AI investments—the company plans to spend as much as $145 billion this year alone on capital expenditures to support those investments—into new sources of revenue. In September, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg unveiled Meta Enterprise Platform, a new business unit focused on selling the company’s broader portfolio of AI products, such as its Muse Code coding tool, business agent software and Muse Spark models, to businesses and developers. Zuckerberg tapped Chirantan “CJ” Desai, the former CEO of software company MongoDB , to lead it, calling the effort the “next major pillar” of Meta’s business. Building an enterprise business has proved elusive for Meta in the past, though. Workplace, a version of Facebook designed for internal company communications, attracted 7 million paid subscribers at its peak in 2021. But it struggled to compete with workplace tools from Microsoft and Slack, and Meta announced that it would discontinue it in 2024. The company also developed virtual reality tools for businesses but later wound down or reworked those offerings. As part of its new push, Meta is turning to the kinds of partnerships that enterprise software and AI firms have long used to get large companies using their products. OpenAI, Anthropic and other companies already rely on large consulting firms to help sell and deploy their products to enterprises. Meta sees relationships with those same firms as a way to make deployments of its AI products inside large customers faster and less reliant on Meta’s engineers, one person familiar with the company’s thinking said. Meta’s new organization emerged after over a year of learning what AI products businesses would and wouldn’t buy from it. In 2024, the company saw an opportunity to use AI agents to address a common problem for businesses: unanswered customer messages. Small and midsize businesses greeted its customer agent offering enthusiastically as the software helped them answer customer questions around the clock, manage inquiries and free up their time, according to people familiar with the matter. Landing larger enterprise deals was a harder nut to crack. Last October, Meta tried to persuade retailers to put its business agent directly on their websites, where it could answer shoppers’ questions and provide customer support. But the pitch ran into resistance from major companies, including Amazon and Booking.com, which were reluctant to give Meta greater access to their customers and already had their own AI initiatives, the people said. Large businesses also wanted more control over how the agents interacted with customers before they were willing to roll them out more broadly. They needed ways to test responses, adjust the agents’ behavior and tone to match their brands, and ensure conversations could be smoothly handed off to human employees when necessary, one of the people said. And there was a more fundamental question of trust. Companies increasingly viewed their customer conversations and the data the agents would need access to as valuable business information, making some reluctant to hand it over to Meta, two of the people said. There was also the technical challenge of giving the agent access to a company’s inventory, pricing, shipping information and other data that is often scattered across separate backend systems. Connecting all of that required help from Meta engineers, who had to work closely with retailers’ technical teams, making deployments more complicated than the company had anticipated, the people said. Meta ultimately shut down its effort to deploy business agents on retailers’ websites in December, two of the people said. It discontinued the product after customers told it consumers weren’t interested in interacting with a chatbot on a retailer’s website, according to one of the people. Despite the reservations some large customers had about using its business agent software, Meta found success getting some of them to use the agents through its messaging platforms, including WhatsApp and Messenger. For example, Movida, a Brazilian car rental company, uses a business agent on WhatsApp, while Indian e-commerce firm Flipkart and Brazilian electronic toll payment company Sem Parar have also signed up for the agents, according to people familiar with the matter. Meta is making progress getting other large companies to use its agent on its messaging apps, according to Fred Leach, Meta’s vice president of product. “We’re pretty excited about the results that we’re going to be able to take to market going into next year, and about all of the AI offerings that we have as a company. I feel like we’re just scratching the surface,” Leach said. In its recent third-quarter earnings call, Meta teased other enterprise offerings on the horizon. Zuckerberg said Meta eventually wants to offer a “business network” of AI agents that can work across corporate environments.
